licoes.c: To contemplate: does a relationship that asks for love under threat of death deserve to be called love? Ask it of any relationship, human ones too.

licoes.t: A God in the image of those who describe him: what psychology says
licoes.r: You cannot diagnose a character in a book; doing so would be as unscientific as calling him perfect. But patterns can be compared. The traits the texts give Yahweh match the ideals of an ancient Near Eastern warrior king: jealousy and a demand for exclusive loyalty (“Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5)), total destruction of the enemy (“And when the LORD thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:” (Deuteronomy 7:2)), collective punishment and reward for the obedient. Modern psychology studies these patterns in people and groups: dehumanization of the out-group (Nick Haslam, 2006), moral disengagement, which is justifying violence by a 'higher' cause (Albert Bandura), and collective punishment.
licoes.a:
And there is direct experimental data: in 2009 Nicholas Epley and colleagues (PNAS) showed that when religious people estimate what God thinks about controversial issues, the answer tracks their own opinion more than the opinion they attribute to others. When their own view shifted, their 'God' shifted with it. A modern hint of something ancient: each generation tends to describe God with its own mind. This fits your intuition, with one correction: not one person, but many generations of scribes, each putting the values and fears of their time into the text. Sources: Epley et al. 2009 — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0908374106 ; moral disengagement — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_disengagement ; dehumanization — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehumanization

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Exodus 20:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+20%3A5&version=KJV | Deuteronomy 7:2 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+7%3A2&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: when someone says 'God wants this', it is worth gently asking: is it God, or me speaking through him?

licoes.t: From Sheol to hell: how eternal punishment was built
licoes.r: For almost the entire Old Testament there is no hell of torment. The dead go to Sheol, a dark, silent place for everyone, good and bad: “For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.” (Ecclesiastes 9:5) “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.” (Ecclesiastes 9:10) And the psalmist asks: “For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks?” (Psalms 6:5) The first clear mention of different fates after death only appears in Daniel, written around 165 BC: “And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.” (Daniel 12:2)
licoes.a:
Between the exile and the time of Jesus, Judaism came into contact with Persian Zoroastrianism (final judgment, resurrection, cosmic battle of good and evil) and with Greek culture (immortal soul, Hades and Tartarus). The idea of punishment grew in that mix. The gospels have “Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:” (Matthew 25:41) “And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.” (Matthew 25:46) and “Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” (Mark 9:48) 'Gehenna' was the valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem, remembered for ancient sacrifices. In Revelation: “And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.” (Revelation 14:11) Bart Ehrman, in 'Heaven and Hell' (2020), traces this evolution step by step. Eternal hell did not 'come from heaven' ready-made: it was built over some 400 years, and it is also the strongest fear tool ever used to obtain obedience. Sources: Sheol — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheol ; Gehenna — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna ; Ehrman — https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Heaven-and-Hell/Bart-D-Ehrman/9781501136757

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Ecclesiastes 9:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ecclesiastes+9%3A5&version=KJV | Ecclesiastes 9:10 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ecclesiastes+9%3A10&version=KJV | Psalms 6:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalms+6%3A5&version=KJV | Daniel 12:2 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Daniel+12%3A2&version=KJV | Matthew 25:41 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+25%3A41&version=KJV | Matthew 25:46 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+25%3A46&version=KJV | Mark 9:48 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+9%3A48&version=KJV | Revelation 14:11 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Revelation+14%3A11&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: the Bible's oldest authors knew no hell. An idea that took centuries to appear was built by people.

licoes.t: Gods who watch and punish: religion and social control
licoes.r: Your intuition that religion served to control has a scientific basis, but the story is fuller. Psychologist Ara Norenzayan, in 'Big Gods' (Princeton, 2013), proposes that all-seeing, punishing gods helped large societies cooperate among strangers: people who feel watched cheat less. A study across 8 societies (Purzycki et al., Nature, 2016) found more generosity toward distant co-religionists among those who believed in a moralizing, punishing god. In the Bible the formula is explicit: obedience brings blessing, and disobedience brings “I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) and “But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:” (Deuteronomy 28:15)
licoes.a:
Scientific honesty: in 2019 a famous Nature study (Whitehouse et al.) claimed societies became complex before moralizing gods appeared. It was criticized for treating missing data as 'absence' (Beheim et al., Nature, 2021) and was retracted. The debate remains open. What is known: belief in a watching, punishing god increases cooperation and obedience within the group, and rulers can use that. But religion also gave identity, comfort in grief, an explanation for disasters and unity in exile. Control was an important function, not the only one. Sources: Norenzayan — https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691169743/big-gods ; Purzycki 2016 — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16980 ; Whitehouse 2019 (retracted) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1043-4 ; Beheim 2021 — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03655-4

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Leviticus 26:16 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Leviticus+26%3A16&version=KJV | Deuteronomy 28:15 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+28%3A15&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: feeling watched changes behaviour. It's worth knowing who holds the camera.

licoes.t: 'God is love' vs the texts: contradictions that invite questions
licoes.r: The Bible also says “He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.” (1 John 4:8), “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.” (Psalms 145:9), “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.” (Luke 6:36) and “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8) And it contradicts itself on inherited guilt. Exodus says “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;” (Exodus 20:5), but Ezekiel answers “The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.” (Ezekiel 18:20) These voices don't fit the massacre orders in the previous lessons. That is what you'd expect from a book written by many people, in different eras, with different ideas about God.
licoes.a:
How believers handle this, to be fair: in the 2nd century Marcion concluded the Old Testament God was a different god, and was declared a heretic. Origen read the massacres as allegories of inner struggle. Today apologists like Paul Copan ('Is God a Moral Monster?', 2011) say the texts use typical ancient war hyperbole, and theologians speak of 'progressive revelation'. Notice that all these answers admit that, read literally, the texts don't match a perfectly loving God. The simplest explanation, accepted by much academic research, is that they reflect the people and eras that wrote them. Sources: Marcion — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcionism ; Copan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Copan ; problem of evil — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problem_of_evil

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): 1 John 4:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+John+4%3A8&version=KJV | Psalms 145:9 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalms+145%3A9&version=KJV | Luke 6:36 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+6%3A36&version=KJV | Micah 6:8 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Micah+6%3A8&version=KJV | Ezekiel 18:20 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezekiel+18%3A20&version=KJV | Exodus 20:5 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+20%3A5&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: you don't have to choose between swallowing everything and throwing it all away. You can keep 'be merciful' and leave the rest as the history of an age.

licoes.t: How a repeated idea becomes 'truth': the illusory truth effect
licoes.r: In 1977 Lynn Hasher and colleagues showed that statements heard several times seem truer than new ones, even when false. This is the illusory truth effect. In 2015 Lisa Fazio and colleagues showed it works even when people know the right answer: repetition creates familiarity, and the brain mistakes familiarity for truth. Add three reinforcers: hearing it from childhood from people we love; seeing adults make costly sacrifices for the faith (anthropologist Joseph Henrich calls these CREDs, 2009); and fear of questioning, when doubt is treated as sin and leaving can cost your family (compare “If thy brother, the son of thy mother, or thy son, or thy daughter, or the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend, which is as thine own soul, entice thee secretly, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, which thou hast not known, thou, nor thy fathers;” (Deuteronomy 13:6)).
licoes.a:
This explains why intelligent, good people believe sincerely. They weren't foolish: they received a story repeated for generations, in an environment that rewarded accepting and punished doubting. A fair point: the effect applies to all of us, to any idea, including our own. The antidote is the same for any belief: go to the source, compare versions, ask 'how would I know if this were false?'. Sources: illusory truth effect — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect ; Fazio et al. 2015 — https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000098 ; Henrich 2009 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2009.03.005

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Deuteronomy 13:6 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Deuteronomy+13%3A6&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: what idea have you never questioned just because you always heard it? Pick one and check the source, without fear.

licoes.t: What is true and what is not: who created the God of the Bible (table)
licoes.r: Scientific sum: 26 claims checked, one per row, with verse and source. Result: ✅ 16 match reality, ❌ 8 don't and ❔ 2 are not verifiable. Matching: many authors over centuries, Yahweh's southern origin, Asherah worship, monotheism born in exile, parallels with Mesha and the Assyrian treaties, what the massacre verses actually say, and the illusory truth effect. Not matching: a single author, one person inventing God to control, Jericho and the flood as narrated, a hell that always existed and a consistent text on inherited guilt. God's existence itself science neither proves nor refutes. Full table as cards: open conteudo/tabela-quem-criou-deus.html?lang=en or see below.
licoes.a:
Format: Claim (verse) · Verdict · Evidence — source. 'Matches reality' on massacre rows means: the text says exactly that.

1. The Bible was written by one person (Moses) or dictated ready-made from heaven (Deuteronomy 34:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   The text narrates Moses' death (Deut 34) and shows sources in different styles written over centuries. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_hypothesis

2. The texts were written and edited by many people over about a thousand years (2 Kings 22:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Academic consensus: J, E, D, P sources/layers and editing in and after the exile. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplementary_hypothesis

3. The 'book of the law' found by Josiah served a religious and political reform (2 Kings 22:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Most scholars link this book to the core of Deuteronomy (7th century BC). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah

4. Yahweh was described as a storm and war god coming from the south (Seir, Edom) (Judges 5:4; Deuteronomy 33:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Ancient biblical texts and Egyptian inscriptions about the 'Shasu of YHW' point to this origin (widely held hypothesis). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh

5. Israelites worshipped a goddess (Asherah, 'queen of heaven') along with Yahweh (Jeremiah 7:18; 2 Kings 23:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Kuntillet Ajrud inscriptions (c. 800 BC): 'Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuntillet_Ajrud

6. Ancient texts speak of a council of gods (Psalms 82:1; Deuteronomy 32:8)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Ps 82 and Deut 32:8 in the Dead Sea Scrolls ('sons of God') echo El's pantheon at Ugarit. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_God

7. Full monotheism gained strength in the Babylonian exile (Isaiah 45:5; Exodus 34:14)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Older texts demand loyalty to one god among others (monolatry); Isa 40–55 (c. 540 BC) denies other gods. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monolatry

8. Neighboring peoples had war gods who ordered cities exterminated (2 Kings 3:27)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC): Chemosh orders the attack on Nebo; 7,000 are 'devoted to destruction'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesha_Stele

9. Deuteronomy uses the model of Assyrian loyalty treaties (Deuteronomy 13:6; Deuteronomy 28:53)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Parallels with Esarhaddon's treaty (672 BC): report relatives, curses of famine and cannibalism. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esarhaddon

10. The text orders killing boys and women and sparing virgins 'for yourselves' (Numbers 31:17; Numbers 31:18)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today: genocide and sexual slavery (Rome Statute, arts. 6, 7 and 8). — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf

11. The text attributes to God orders to leave no survivors, including children (Deuteronomy 20:16; 1 Samuel 15:3)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today: genocide and a war crime (arts. 6 and 8.2.b.xii). — https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/RS-Eng.pdf

12. The conquest of Jericho happened as narrated (Joshua 6:21)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Jericho was practically uninhabited at the time attributed to Joshua (Kenyon; Finkelstein). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho

13. A worldwide flood killed all land life outside the ark (Genesis 7:23)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   There is no global geological layer from a recent flood; see the theme 'The math of the flood'. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_geology

14. All the firstborn of Egypt died in one night (Exodus 12:29)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   There is no Egyptian record or archaeological evidence of the Exodus as narrated. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exodus

15. The text orders killing even a relative who invites you to worship another god (Deuteronomy 13:6; Deuteronomy 13:10)
   ✅ Matches reality
   It is written so. Today it would violate the right to life and freedom of religion (ICCPR, arts. 6 and 18). — https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights

16. The Bible always taught a hell of eternal torment (Ecclesiastes 9:5; Psalms 6:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   In the Old Testament the dead go to Sheol, for all; different fates only appear in Daniel (c. 165 BC). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheol

17. The idea of eternal hell developed under Persian and Greek influences (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Zoroastrianism (final judgment) and Hellenism (immortal soul, Tartarus); Ehrman, 'Heaven and Hell' (2020). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gehenna

18. Belief in a watching, punishing god increases obedience and cooperation in the group (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:15)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Purzycki et al., Nature 2016; Norenzayan, 'Big Gods' (2013). — https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16980

19. Moralizing gods appeared only after societies became complex (Leviticus 26:16)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   The 2019 study (Whitehouse, Nature) was retracted after critiques; the question remains open. — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03655-4

20. A single person deliberately invented God to control the people (Exodus 20:5)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It took many generations; control was one function, alongside identity, comfort and explaining disasters. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origins_of_Judaism

21. The traits of the God of the texts mirror the ideals of warrior kings of that age (Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 7:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Exclusive loyalty, extermination of the enemy and curses also appear in Mesha and Assyrian treaties. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herem_(war_or_property)

22. People tend to attribute their own opinions to God (Exodus 20:5)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Epley et al., PNAS 2009: estimates of 'what God thinks' track the person's own opinion. — https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.0908374106

23. The Bible is consistent about punishing children for their parents' sins (Exodus 20:5; Ezekiel 18:20)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Ex 20:5 says yes; Ezek 18:20 says no. They are different voices. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Ezekiel

24. 'God is love' fits, read literally, with the massacre orders (1 John 4:8; Numbers 31:17)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Even apologists and theologians resort to allegory, hyperbole or progressive revelation to reconcile them. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcionism

25. An idea repeated many times seems truer (Deuteronomy 13:6)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Illusory truth effect (Hasher 1977; Fazio et al. 2015). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect

26. There is a God behind the texts (1 John 4:8)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   Science neither proves nor refutes it. What it shows is that the image of God in the texts was shaped by people. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_of_God

licoes.t: Conhecimento Solar's opinion: honest verdict on who created the God of the Bible
p: was the god of the bible invented
licoes.r: Verdict: the image of God in the Bible was written by human beings, and that matches reality. Many hands over about a thousand years: tribes with a storm god from the south, kings who needed loyalty, priests in exile who turned defeat into 'punishment for sins', and later teachers who, under Persian and Greek influence, created eternal hell. This God's harshest traits (jealousy, exclusive loyalty, collective punishment, extermination of the enemy) are those of the kings and war gods of the age, as on the Mesha Stele and in Assyrian treaties. A human giving the orders of Numbers 31 or 1 Samuel 15 today would be tried for genocide. And the same book also says 'God is love' and 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father'. They are different human voices that don't agree with each other.
licoes.a:
Where your intuition needs adjusting: it wasn't one person, and control through fear and guilt was a real function, but not the only one. These texts also gave identity, comfort and hope to a small, threatened people. Science neither proves nor refutes that a God exists. What it shows is that the biblical portrait of God bears the marks of those who drew it. Believers were not foolish: they received a story repeated for generations (illusory truth effect — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusory_truth_effect). A calm invitation: read the cited verses in context, check the sources and decide freely, without fear. licoes.c: To contemplate: if the image of God was painted by people, you too can choose which values to keep: mercy, justice, care for others, without needing fear.

licoes.t: Genesis put to the test: what we've seen and what was missing
licoes.r: This theme completes what the Portal has already shown, without repeating it. Already covered elsewhere: the six days, Genesis 1 × Genesis 2, the single couple and genetics, the rib, the serpent and biology, Cain's wife and the 930 years (theme 'Adam and Eve'); the ark and the water (theme 'The math of the flood'); who wrote the Bible, where Yahweh came from and the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); and dozens of contradictions (theme 'Contradictions, atrocities and manipulation'). Here come the missing pieces: why an all-knowing God asks questions, how the serpent became Satan, why there are talking animals, what the text doesn't explain about Cain and Abel, whether God or people wrote the Bible, and why children accept what they hear as absolute truth.
licoes.a:
The method is the same for each point, step by step: 1) what the text says, with the full verse; 2) what science, history and archaeology show; 3) what is myth, meaning a narrative that conveys meaning but doesn't describe facts; 4) what still has value. Myth here is not an insult: it is a literary genre, like the fable or the parable. At the end comes a summary table with what matches reality, what doesn't and what can't be verified. One rule of respect holds throughout: sincere believers are neither foolish nor bad. The question is about the text, not about the person's worth. The Bible itself gives permission to examine: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:21)

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): 1 Thessalonians 5:21 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Thessalonians+5%3A21&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: examining is not destroying. It is separating what you received from what you confirmed.

licoes.t: Why does an all-knowing God ask questions?
licoes.r: Right after the fruit, the text says “And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). And goes on: “And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” (Genesis 3:11). To the woman: “And the LORD God said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.” (Genesis 3:13). With Cain, the same: “And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?” (Genesis 4:9). Yet another text in the same Bible says “For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.” (Psalms 139:4). If God knows everything, why ask where someone is, or where the murdered brother is?
licoes.a:
There are three main readings, and all deserve respect. 1) Historical reading: Genesis 2 to 4 comes from the source scholars call the Yahwist (J), which describes God in very human terms: he shapes clay, walks in the garden 'in the cool of the day' (Gen 3:8) and makes garments of skin (Gen 3:21). In this portrait, God really seems to find things out. Omniscience appears in other texts, like Psalm 139, and was systematized later by theology. 2) Traditional Jewish reading: Rashi (11th century) says on Gen 3:9 that God knew where Adam was, but asked to open a conversation, so he would not be terrified by a sudden punishment; he says the same of 'Where is Abel?'. 3) Christian teaching reading: the question is an invitation to repentance, not a request for information. Honest conclusion: readings 2 and 3 resolve the tension through interpretation; the text, read as it stands, shows a God who asks like someone who doesn't know. Sources: Rashi on Gen 3:9 — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.3.9 ; Yahwist — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist ; anthropomorphism — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism

licoes.c: To contemplate: a good question isn't meant to catch someone out. It helps the person find themselves. Where are you?

licoes.t: 'I will go down and see': the God who has to check
p: i will go down and see
now i know that you fear god
tower of babel god came down
licoes.r: Elsewhere, God seems to need to see in order to know. At the tower of Babel: “And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.” (Genesis 11:5). About Sodom: “I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know.” (Genesis 18:21). And after ordering Abraham to sacrifice his son: “And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.” (Genesis 22:12). 'Now I know' implies that before, he did not.
licoes.a:
The readings: Rashi, on Gen 18:21, reads 'I will go down' as a lesson for judges: do not decide life-and-death cases without first examining carefully. Classical theologians such as Boethius and Thomas Aquinas teach that God knows everything at once, outside time, and that these texts speak 'in human fashion'. Open theism, a modern Christian current, reads these passages more literally: free choices would not yet be settled, not even for God. Scholars note that the image of a God who lives on high and 'comes down' to look at the earth is typical of the region's ancient narratives. What doesn't match: a God who knows everything and, in the same book, a God who must come down, look and test in order to know. Both images are in the text; later theology is what joins them. Sources: Rashi on Gen 18:21 — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.18.21 ; open theism — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_theism ; omniscience — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omniscience

licoes.c: To contemplate: even in the sacred text, the one who will judge goes to look closely first. Do you check before you condemn?

licoes.t: From serpent to Satan: how the snake became the devil
licoes.r: In Genesis, the serpent is an animal: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?” (Genesis 3:1). Its punishment is an animal's too: crawling and eating dust (Gen 3:14), and enmity between snakes and people: “And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15). The name Satan appears nowhere in Genesis. In the Hebrew Bible, 'satan' means 'adversary' or 'accuser', and appears as a member of the heavenly court: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them.” (Job 1:6). In Zechariah he accuses the high priest: “And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him.” (Zechariah 3:1). The link between the serpent and the devil appears centuries later: in the book of Wisdom (around the 1st century BC), 'by the envy of the devil, death came into the world' (Wis 2:24); and in the last book of the New Testament: “And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.” (Revelation 12:9).
licoes.a:
Why this matters: the story many learn as children ('Satan, disguised as a snake, deceived Eve') is a later reading laid over the text. Many scholars link the growth of the Satan figure to the period when Jews lived under the Persian Empire, whose religion (Zoroastrianism) had an evil spirit, Angra Mainyu, fighting the good god. This is a much-debated hypothesis, not a proven fact. Christians, from Irenaeus (2nd century) on, also read Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of Christ, the 'protoevangelium'; in context, the verse speaks of people and snakes as enemies. Sources: Satan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan ; serpents in the Bible — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpents_in_the_Bible ; Wisdom 2:24 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Wisdom+2%3A24&version=DRA ; protoevangelium — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protevangelium

licoes.c: To contemplate: sometimes the enemy we were taught to fear was added later. What other fears did you inherit without checking?

licoes.t: Talking animals: the serpent, the donkey and ancient fables
licoes.r: The Bible has two talking animals: the serpent in Eden and Balaam's donkey: “And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?” (Numbers 22:28). In biology this doesn't happen: speech requires a vocal apparatus able to articulate sounds and brain areas for language. Snakes have no vocal cords and only hiss; donkeys bray but don't form words. In the ancient world, though, the talking animal was a well-known storytelling device. In Egypt, the 'Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor', from the Middle Kingdom (about 4,000 years ago), has a giant serpent that talks with a sailor. And the fables attributed to Aesop (6th century BC) use talking animals to teach lessons.
licoes.a:
In the Bible itself, the serpent has another curious role. Moses makes a bronze serpent that heals whoever looks at it: “And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” (Numbers 21:9). Centuries later, King Hezekiah destroys it, because the people were burning incense to it: “He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.” (2 Kings 18:4). In other words, there was worship of a serpent in Israel. In several cultures of the region, the serpent symbolized healing, renewed life (it sheds its skin), wisdom and also chaos. This helps explain why it appears in Eden as more 'subtil' than any beast. Conclusion: the talking serpent doesn't match zoology; as a fable, it speaks of temptation, desire and responsibility. Sources: Shipwrecked Sailor — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tale_of_the_Shipwrecked_Sailor ; Nehushtan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nehushtan ; Balaam's donkey — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaam%27s_ass ; Aesop's Fables — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesop%27s_Fables

licoes.c: To contemplate: a fable isn't a lie when everyone knows it's a fable. The problem starts when it's taught as a news report.

licoes.t: Cain and Abel: why was one offering accepted and not the other?
licoes.r: Abel offers animals from the flock and Cain, fruit of the ground: “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering:” (Genesis 4:4) “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” (Genesis 4:5). The text doesn't explain why God preferred one offering. Explanations came later: the New Testament says “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh.” (Hebrews 11:4) and “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.” (1 John 3:12). Ancient interpreters noticed that Abel brought 'the firstlings' and 'the fat', and Cain only 'of the fruit', and concluded that Cain gave half-heartedly. Before the crime, God warns: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” (Genesis 4:7). After the crime: “And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.” (Genesis 4:10).
licoes.a:
Historical reading: many scholars see here the clash between two ways of life, the shepherd's and the farmer's, who lived side by side and competed for land and water in the Near East. There is a Sumerian poem, 'Dumuzid and Enkimdu', in which a shepherd and a farmer compete for the goddess Inana: she prefers the farmer, her brother speaks up for the shepherd, and in the end the two make peace. It is a thematic parallel, not proof of copying. The difference stands out: in the Sumerian poem the dispute ends in friendship; in Genesis, in blood. What matches reality: herding and farming began in the Neolithic, about 11,000 years ago, and conflicts between these groups are real. What doesn't: the first couple's first sons already being a shepherd and a farmer, when our species is about 300,000 years old, almost all of it lived as hunter-gatherers. Cain's wife and the city of Enoch are already in the theme 'Adam and Eve'. Sources: Dumuzid and Enkimdu (University of Oxford translation) — https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/section4/tr40833.htm ; Cain and Abel — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cain_and_Abel ; Neolithic Revolution — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution

licoes.c: To contemplate: 'Am I my brother's keeper?' The answer the story asks for, and life does too, is yes.

licoes.t: The mark of Cain: from protection to an excuse for racism
licoes.r: In the text, the mark of Cain is a protection: “And the LORD said unto him, Therefore whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold. And the LORD set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.” (Genesis 4:15). Genesis doesn't say what the mark was and says nothing about skin color. Even so, from at least the 1730s in the United States, the idea spread that Black people descended from Cain and that dark skin was the 'curse'. This was used to justify slavery and discrimination. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, for example, did not ordain Black men from 1852 until 1978. Today it officially disavows the theory that black skin is a sign of a curse.
licoes.a:
A detail that touches Brazil: the church itself says, in its official essay, that Black and mixed-ancestry members helped build the São Paulo temple, which they would not be allowed to enter, and that this weighed on the 1978 change. This is an example of how a reading called 'the word of God' can shield a human prejudice: the text didn't say it, but once placed as sacred it seemed beyond question. Something similar happened with Genesis 9:25, the 'curse of Canaan', already covered in the theme 'Contradictions'. The good news: the churches themselves revised these readings as moral conscience advanced. It shows that interpretation changes with people, and that people were always part of what was called 'God's will'. Sources: essay 'Race and the Priesthood' — https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/gospel-topics-essays/race-and-the-priesthood?lang=eng ; mark of Cain — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_and_mark_of_Cain ; David Goldenberg, 'The Curse of Ham' (Princeton, 2003)

Verses cited (check the text) (King James Version, public domain): Genesis 4:15 — https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis+4%3A15&version=KJV
licoes.c: To contemplate: when a 'sacred truth' hurts someone for being born as they were, the question isn't against God. It is for the human being.

licoes.t: Did God write the Bible, or did people write in God's name?
p: is the bible the word of god
licoes.r: The Bible itself shows people speaking in God's name, and admits that this could be false. Jeremiah accuses: “How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain.” (Jeremiah 8:8) (modern translations: 'the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie'). And also: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 23:16). In other words, even then there were people saying 'thus says the Lord' with ideas from their own heads, and the text recognizes it. The formula wasn't unique to Israel: in the letters from the city of Mari, in Syria (around 1770 BC), prophets brought King Zimri-Lim messages beginning 'Thus says Dagan' or 'Thus says Adad', the gods there.
licoes.a:
What history shows: the books were written by people, in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, over about a thousand years, and the list of books was decided gradually (see 'Who wrote the Bible' and 'Who chose the books of the Bible'). Other books also claim to come from God: the Quran, the Book of Mormon and the Vedas, called in India 'shruti', 'that which was heard'. They contradict one another, so the sentence 'this book came from God' cannot prove itself; if it could, all of them would be true at once. The circular reasoning usually goes: 'the Bible is God's word because it says so' (“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:” (2 Timothy 3:16)). Science can neither prove nor disprove that someone was inspired. What can be checked is the content: when the text describes the world (the age of the Earth, the order of creation, a global flood), it shows the knowledge of its writers' time, not knowledge only God would have. Sources: prophecy at Mari — https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/16/11/1400 ; circular reasoning — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_reasoning ; biblical inspiration — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_inspiration

licoes.c: To contemplate: if someone says 'God sent me to tell you this', ask calmly: how could I check?

licoes.t: Why a 'sacred' book feels like absolute truth
licoes.r: When an idea is called sacred, the mind starts treating it differently. Psychologist Philip Tetlock (2003) described 'sacred values': things people refuse to weigh against anything else, and which provoke outrage at the mere thought of questioning them. Scott Atran and Jeremy Ginges (Science, 2012) showed that sacred values resist arguments and even material offers. That's why a text declared sacred stops being read as 'what someone wrote' and starts being read as 'what is'.
licoes.a:
Three mechanisms combined: 1) authority: we learn from those we trust (parents, pastor, priest), and questioning feels like betrayal; 2) repetition: the illusory truth effect (theme 'Who created the God of the Bible?'); 3) the cost of doubting: fear of punishment and of losing family and community. The text sometimes protects itself: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.” (Deuteronomy 4:2). This was common in ancient texts: the Code of Hammurabi ends with curses on anyone who alters or erases its laws. None of this proves the content false, nor true. It only shows that the feeling of absolute certainty comes from the 'sacred' label and the group, not from verification. Sources: Tetlock 2003 — https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(03)00135-9 ; Atran and Ginges 2012 — https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1216902 ; Code of Hammurabi — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi

licoes.t: Sponge mind: why children accept what they hear as truth
licoes.r: A child has no way to check alone whether God exists, whether the world is 6,000 years old or whether there is a hell. Children learn through adults' testimony. Paul Harris and Melissa Koenig (Child Development, 2006) showed that children learn scientific things they can't see (the Earth is round, germs exist) and religious things (God, heaven) in the same way: by trusting the speaker. In a 2015 study, Kathleen Corriveau, Eva Chen and Paul Harris told stories to 5- and 6-year-olds. In religious stories with miracles, children who went to church or attended a religious school said the character was real; children from non-religious families said it was made up. The religious children also more often accepted fantastical stories as real.
licoes.a:
This doesn't mean children believe anyone: from age 3 or 4 they prefer informants who were right before (Koenig and Harris, 2005). The point is different: when all the trusted adults say the same thing from early on, a child cannot know that it is one belief among many. Psychologist Daniel Gilbert (1991) showed that even in adults, understanding a sentence comes with believing it for a moment; doubting takes a second step, with effort and information. The Bible itself knows this power: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” (Proverbs 22:6) and “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.” (Deuteronomy 6:7). And Paul describes growing up: “When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.” (1 Corinthians 13:11). This is neither a diagnosis nor an accusation: parents who teach faith usually do so out of love and conviction. Sources: Harris and Koenig 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00886.x ; Corriveau, Chen and Harris 2015 — https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.12138 ; Koenig and Harris 2005 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2005.00849.x ; Gilbert 1991 — https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.46.2.107 ; Paul Harris, 'Trusting What You're Told' (Harvard, 2012) — https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674503830

licoes.t: If you had been born somewhere else: religion and birthplace
p: if i was born in another country
religion depends on where you are born
why do i follow my parents religion
licoes.r: The religion a person follows depends heavily on where and to whom they were born. In the Pew Research Center survey of 36 countries (published in 2025, nearly 80,000 people), in India, Israel, Nigeria and Thailand, 95% or more of adults remain in the religious group they were raised in. Even where switching is more common, most stay: in Brazil, 21% no longer identify with their childhood religion, so about 4 in 5 remain in it. Someone born into a Hindu family in India almost always stays Hindu; into a Jewish family in Israel, Jewish; into a Catholic or evangelical family in Brazil, most likely Christian.
licoes.a:
Think it through: a boy born in Varanasi, India, to Hindu parents, grows up sure that Krishna is real; a boy born in Goiânia, Brazil, to evangelical parents, grows up sure that Jesus is the only way. Both are sincere, with the same kind of certainty, and each finds the other's belief strange. The sincerity is equal; what changes is the address. This doesn't prove that no religion is true, but it shows that the certainty we feel comes largely from place and family, not from having compared the options. And the map itself changes over time: until the 1970s, over 90% of Brazilians called themselves Catholic; in the 2022 IBGE census, 56.7% did, with 26.9% evangelical and 9.3% with no religion. Sources: Pew Research Center 2025 — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/ ; IBGE, 2022 census — https://agenciagov.ebc.com.br/noticias/202506/censo-2022-catolicos-seguem-em-queda-evangelicos-e-sem-religiao-crescem-no-pais ; BBC Brasil — https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/articles/crk2p5xr0m7o

licoes.c: To contemplate: had you been born on the other side of the world, what would you believe with the same certainty? What is left of you when the address is removed?

licoes.t: Teaching to believe or teaching to think: the difference
licoes.r: Educating means teaching content and also how to evaluate it. Indoctrinating, according to philosopher of education I. A. Snook ('Indoctrination and Education', 1972), means teaching with the intention that the person believe regardless of the evidence. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) guarantees the child freedom of thought, conscience and religion (article 14), and says parents provide direction in a manner consistent with the child's evolving capacities.
licoes.a:
In practice, the difference shows when a question comes. A child asks: 'Why did God ask where Adam was, if he knows everything?'. An answer that educates: 'Good question; there are several readings, let's look together'. An answer that indoctrinates: 'You don't question God's word'. The first shapes someone who thinks; the second, someone who obeys fear. The Bible has advice that fits here: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Signs of indoctrination, without diagnosing anyone: doubt is treated as sin; other religions appear only as error or demons; fear of hell and punishment is used to keep the belief; leaving the group means losing your family. Signs of education: open sources, other views presented with respect and freedom to change one's mind. Sources: Convention on the Rights of the Child — https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/convention-rights-child ; indoctrination — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indoctrination

licoes.c: To contemplate: faith born of answered questions weighs differently from faith born of the fear of asking.

licoes.t: What matches and what doesn't: Genesis put to the test (table)
p: genesis put to the test table
what is myth in the bible
licoes.r: This theme's sum: 24 claims checked, one per row, with verse and source. Result: ✅ 11 match reality, ❌ 10 don't and ❔ 3 are not verifiable. Matching: Satan as an accuser in the Hebrew Bible, the bronze serpent cult, the 'human' God of the oldest layer, the clash of shepherds and farmers, the racist use of verses, prophets speaking 'a vision of their own heart', the 'thus says the god' formula at Mari, the effect of the 'sacred' label, children's trust in adults and religion inherited from birth. Not matching: talking animals, snakes eating dust, the serpent as Satan in Genesis, a consistent text about an all-knowing God, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation, the mark of Cain as dark skin and the idea that most people chose their religion by comparing. Full table as cards: open conteudo/tabela-genesis-a-prova.html?lang=en or see below.
licoes.a:
Format: Claim (verse) · Verdict · Evidence — source. For the rest of Genesis (six days, single couple, rib, flood), see the tables in the themes 'Adam and Eve' and 'The math of the flood'.

1. A serpent spoke and argued with a woman (Genesis 3:1)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Snakes have no vocal cords nor a brain for language; talking animals are a fable device. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake

2. In the Genesis text, the serpent was Satan in disguise (Genesis 3:1; Revelation 12:9)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Genesis calls it a 'beast of the field'; the link to the devil appears centuries later (Wis 2:24; Rev 12:9). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan

3. In the Hebrew Bible, 'satan' was an accuser in the heavenly court, not the king of hell (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1)
   ✅ Matches reality
   That is what Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 show. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan

4. Snakes eat dust (Genesis 3:14)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   All snakes are carnivores. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake

5. Israelites came to burn incense to a bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; 2 Kings 18:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   The text itself says Hezekiah destroyed it for that reason. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nehushtan

6. A donkey spoke to Balaam (Numbers 22:28)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Donkeys can't articulate words; the account has the form of an exemplary tale. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balaam%27s_ass

7. In the oldest layer of the text, God is described in human terms: he asks, walks, comes down to see (Genesis 3:9; Genesis 11:5)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Anthropomorphism typical of the Yahwist source (J). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist

8. The Bible is consistent about God knowing everything (Psalms 139:4; Genesis 22:12)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Ps 139 says he knows everything; Gen 18:21 and 22:12 show a God who must see in order to know. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omniscience

9. God asked only to open a conversation or to teach (Rashi) (Genesis 3:9; Genesis 18:21)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   A possible faith reading; the intention cannot be verified. — https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Genesis.3.9

10. Genesis explains why God accepted Abel and rejected Cain (Genesis 4:5; Hebrews 11:4)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It doesn't; the reasons (faith, a better offering) were given later (Heb 11:4; 1 Jn 3:12). — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cain_and_Abel

11. Shepherds and farmers lived side by side and competed in the Near East (Genesis 4:4)
   ✅ Matches reality
   The Neolithic (~11,000 years) and the Sumerian poem 'Dumuzid and Enkimdu'. — https://etcsl.orinst.ox.ac.uk/section4/tr40833.htm

12. Cain and Abel were humanity's second generation, already a shepherd and a farmer (Genesis 4:4; Genesis 4:14)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Homo sapiens is ~300,000 years old, almost all of it as hunter-gatherers before farming. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_human

13. The mark of Cain was dark skin (Genesis 4:15)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   The text doesn't say what it was; the racist reading came centuries later and is now rejected even by churches that used it. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_and_mark_of_Cain

14. Readings called 'biblical' were used to justify slavery and racism (Genesis 4:15)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Official Latter-day Saint essay; Goldenberg, 'The Curse of Ham' (2003). — https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/gospel-topics-essays/race-and-the-priesthood?lang=eng

15. The Bible itself admits scribes and prophets spoke in God's name with their own ideas (Jeremiah 8:8; Jeremiah 23:16)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Jeremiah 8:8 and 23:16. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Jeremiah

16. 'Thus says the god' was a common prophetic formula in the ancient Near East (Jeremiah 23:16)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Mari letters (c. 1770 BC): 'Thus says Dagan', 'Thus says Adad'. — https://www.mdpi.com/2077-1444/16/11/1400

17. Saying 'this book came from God' proves it came from God (2 Timothy 3:16)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   It's circular reasoning; other books claim the same and contradict each other. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_reasoning

18. The Bible's authors were inspired by God (2 Timothy 3:16)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   A statement of faith: science neither proves nor refutes it. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_inspiration

19. Calling a text sacred makes it resistant to questions and arguments (Deuteronomy 4:2)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Sacred values: Tetlock 2003; Atran and Ginges, Science 2012. — https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1216902

20. Children accept as real what trusted adults teach, miracles included (Proverbs 22:6)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Harris and Koenig 2006; Corriveau, Chen and Harris 2015. — https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.12138

21. A person's religion depends heavily on where and to whom they were born (Deuteronomy 6:7)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Pew 2025: in several countries 95% or more keep their childhood religion; in Brazil, ~4 in 5. — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/

22. Most people chose their religion after comparing the others (Deuteronomy 6:7; 1 Corinthians 13:11)
   ❌ Does not match reality
   Most receive it in childhood, before being able to compare; certainty comes from the surroundings. — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/

23. It is possible to respect faith and examine the text at the same time (1 Thessalonians 5:21)
   ✅ Matches reality
   Many believing scholars use the historical-critical method. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_criticism

24. There is a God behind the texts (1 John 4:8)
   ❔ Not verifiable
   Science neither proves nor refutes it. What it shows is that the texts bear the marks of their writers. — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_of_God

licoes.t: Conhecimento Solar's opinion: honest verdict on Genesis and belief
licoes.r: Verdict: as an account of facts, Genesis does not match reality. The talking serpent, the talking donkey, the snake that eats dust, Cain and Abel as humanity's second generation: none of it agrees with biology, genetics or archaeology. The text itself shows human hands: in one layer, a God who asks and comes down to see; in another, a God who knows everything; a serpent that became Satan only centuries later; and prophets who, according to Jeremiah, spoke 'a vision of their own heart'. Psychology explains why, even so, so many people feel these stories as absolute truth: they learned them in childhood, from people they loved, in a setting where the book was called sacred and doubting was dangerous. Had they been born in another country, they would feel the same certainty about another book.
licoes.a:
Where care is needed: science neither proves nor refutes that God exists, nor that someone was inspired. What it shows is that the content of these texts reflects the knowledge and values of their writers, in an age without modern science. Myth is not garbage: Genesis carries deep questions about responsibility ('where art thou?'), guilt, envy and caring for one's brother. And sincere believers are not foolish: they received a story with love, from people they trusted. A calm invitation: separate three things, what the text says, what actually happened and what you choose to keep. Read the full verses, check the sources and decide freely, without fear. Sources: Harris and Koenig 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00886.x ; Pew Research Center 2025 — https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/03/26/around-the-world-many-people-are-leaving-their-childhood-religions/ ; Satan — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan ; Yahwist — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jahwist

licoes.c: To contemplate: the key is not trading one inherited certainty for another. It is earning the right to ask and the courage to hear the answer.

licoes.r: Co-creation is aligning intent, emotion and action. In spiritual traditions, you participate in the creation of your reality along with something greater. In practice, nothing is created without action.
licoes.a: Inner reading: cocreating is not giving orders to the universe, it's not fighting it. The Tao Te Ching calls it wu wei, the effortless, forced action, like water surrounding a stone. The Dhammapada opens like this: the mind precedes all things. Practice: Write down an intention today, feel it in your body for a minute, and take a single concrete action in that direction before you go to sleep.
licoes.c: To contemplate: who is the self you want to co-create? If desire is born of fear, it creates more fear; if it is born of wholeness, it creates wholeness. The most subtle lesson is this: the highest work of co-creation is not what you achieve, it's who you become along the way.

licoes.r: The Law of Attraction says that like attracts like: thoughts and emotions would attract experiences. It comes from the 19th-century New Thought movement and was made famous by the 2006 film The Secret. There's no scientific proof that thinking alone attracts things.
licoes.a: Inner reading: what's real is that attention chooses what you see. He who searches for exits finds exits, persists more and does better. So the traditions speak of faith, but always along with works. Beware of the shadow of this idea: Never blame the sufferer for bringing his own pain. Practice: replace the request with the question, what step would I take today if I already trusted the path? And take the step.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the deepest attraction is not that of things, it is that of meaning. You become what you pay attention to every day. What, today, is getting your attention that you didn't choose?

licoes.r: Intention is the seed. A clear, written, repeated intention guides your attention, and attention guides your life.
licoes.a: Inner reading: In the tradition of the Upanishads it is said that you are your deepest desire, for as is the desire, so is the will, and as is the will, so is the act. Practice: Write the intention in the present, short and true, for example: I take care of my body every day. Read it when you wake up and when you sleep, and try it today with a little action.
licoes.c: To contemplate: behind every intention there is a deeper intention. Ask five times, why do I want that? In the fifth answer usually appears what the soul really asks for.

licoes.r: Visualizing is practicing in your mind. Athletes have been using it for decades: the mind trains the path before the body. Studies show that visualizing the process and the obstacles works better than visualizing the trophy alone.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen called it mental contrast: imagine the wish fulfilled, then the most likely inner obstacle, and the plan for when it will appear. The alchemists spoke of true imagination, the imaginatio, as the force that gives form. Practice: close your eyes for two minutes, see the outcome, see the obstacle, and say, "If this happens, I'll do that".
licoes.c: To contemplate: every visualization uses images that you already have. What can you still not imagine for yourself? There's your current limit, and your next growth.

licoes.r: Gratitude is the quickest shortcut to inner abundance. A grateful man sees what he already has.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Cicero wrote, in his Pro Plancio speech, that gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the mother of all others. Gratitude shifts the center of the missing self to the receiving self. Research in positive psychology associates the habit of writing down gratitude with increased well-being. Practice: Tonight, write down three very specific things and in one of them, why it happened.
licoes.c: To ponder: Is it possible to be thankful for what has hurt you? Not for the pain in you, but for what she opened up in you. When gratitude reaches that point, it ceases to be technical and becomes state.

licoes.r: Affirmations are phrases that train the mind. They work best when they're believable to you and come with action. A 2009 study by Joanne Wood showed that exaggerated sentences can worsen the mood of those with low self-esteem.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the word only has power when the whole being agrees with it. If a statement sounds like a lie, the mind resists. In exchange I am rich because I am learning to take care of my money: a truth in the making convinces more than a fantasy. Practice: Write an affirmation that you can say by looking into your own eyes, in the mirror, without deviating.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the strongest affirmation is not about what you'll have, it's about who you are. I am, said silently, without anything afterwards, is one of the oldest phrases in contemplation.

licoes.r: In spiritual language, vibration is your inner state: what you feel and emanate. In physics, vibration is something else, measured in hertz, and the two should not be confused. There is no device that can measure the frequency of the soul.
licoes.a: Inner reading: what traditions call vibration is the quality of your presence. People feel when you're whole or divided. Raising the vibration, in practice, is taking care of sleep, body, company and thoughts. Practice: Before you enter a place today, take three breaths and choose the state you're going in.
licoes.c: To contemplate: you don't have to vibrate loud all the time. Serenity is not a peak, it's a bottom. What about you stays calm even when your moods go up and down?

licoes.r: Abundance starts as a mindset: seeing possibilities instead of just lack. But a mindset without strategy becomes just wishful thinking. Real prosperity comes from spending less than you earn, creating value and having patience.
licoes.a: Inside Reading: Jesus said, in Matthew six, where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. True poverty is when you never feel enough, even when you're full. Practice: Write down everything you spend for a week; abundance begins with clarity. And be wary of anyone who promises wealth in exchange for your money.
licoes.c: To contemplate: how much is enough? If you can't answer, you'll never get there. The highest abundance is needing little and having much to give.

licoes.r: Detachment is not giving up. It's about acting with total dedication and letting go of control over the outcome. Buddhism teaches that much of suffering stems from attachment.
licoes.a: Inner reading: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says to Arjuna: You are entitled to action, but never to its fruits. This is not indifference, it is freedom: you do your best and do not enslave yourself to the result. Practice: pick something you control too much, an outcome, a person, an opinion, and do your part today and let go of the rest.
licoes.c: For contemplation, what would you be afraid to let go of? The answer shows where your prison is. It's not about losing what you love, it's about loving without holding on.

licoes.r: Hermeticism is a philosophical tradition attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus. Its ancient texts, the Corpus Hermeticum, were written in Greek in Roman Egypt around the second and third centuries. The 1908 Caibalion summarizes seven principles: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender.
licoes.a: Important fact: The Caibalion is a modern book, signed by Three Initiates and usually attributed to William Walker Atkinson of New Thought. It's not a thousand-year-old Egyptian text. The Corpus Hermeticum, on the other hand, is ancient and speaks of something else: the mind, the Nous, which illuminates the human being so that he recognizes himself as coming from the divine. Practice: Read one principle a day and note where it appears in your life.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Poimandres, the first book of the Corpus Hermeticum, teaches that he who knows himself walks back to the divine. Principles aren't rules to control the world, they're mirrors for you to see yourself in. Name a principle, for example, the principle of rhythm.

licoes.r: First principle of the Caibalion: Everything is Mind; the Universe is mental. For hermetics, reality arises from a universal consciousness.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Plotinus, in the third century, taught something similar, that everything emanates from the One through Intelligence, the Nous. In practice, the lesson is this: the way you think shapes the way you live, and psychology partly confirms that. On the other hand, the idea that the entire universe is mind is a philosophical assertion, not a proven one. Practice: Today, when a heavy thought comes, say to yourself: This is a thought, not a fact.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if the Whole is Mind, then your silence is also part of it. Who are you in the interval between two thoughts?

p: on earth as it is in heaven
assim na terra como no ceu
licoes.r: Second principle: what's above is like what's below. The phrase comes from the Emerald Tablet. There are patterns that repeat at various levels, from the individual to society.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the ancients spoke of the human being as a microcosm, a small universe that mirrors the big one. Use it as a mirror: Your outer world often reflects your inner world. It's a symbolic lens, not a law of physics. Practice: Clean up a small area of your home today and notice what's lining up inside you.
licoes.c: To contemplate: what's inside is like what's outside. What part of your outer life is screaming something your inner one hasn't yet wanted to hear?

licoes.r: Principle three: nothing is stationary; everything moves; everything vibrates. Heraclitus, 500 years before Christ, taught that everything flows.
licoes.a: Honestly, in physics, atoms vibrate and particles are excitations of fields, but for different reasons and measured in the lab. Hermeticism uses this as a metaphor for mental states: raising the vibration is changing the inner state. Practice: When you feel a heavy state, move your body first, get up, walk, breathe, and watch your mind go along.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if everything changes, no state of yours is final. Not today's sorrow, not yesterday's glory. What about you observes this change without changing?

licoes.r: Fourth principle: everything is double; opposites are identical in nature and different in degree. Hot and cold are the same temperature in different degrees.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Heraclitus said that the way up and down is one. Fear and courage are the same energy at opposite poles: you don't eliminate fear, you move it, degree by degree. The hermetics called it mental transmutation. Practice: name what you're feeling right now and ask, what's the next degree, a little closer to the opposite pole?
licoes.c: To contemplate: he who hates something strongly is attached to it as much as he who loves. Freedom is not in a pole, it's in who sees them both.

licoes.r: Fifth principle: everything flows and flows back; everything has its tides. After the fall comes the climb. The book of Ecclesiastes says the same thing: There is an appointed time for everything.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the wise man neither deludes himself at the top nor despairs at the bottom. He knows that the pendulum turns and stays in the center. Caibalion calls it neutralizing the rhythm: not getting carried away by it. Practice: Today, when a wave comes, of euphoria or discouragement, say quietly: this too passes, and return to the center of the chest.
licoes.c: To contemplate: In what season of life are you now, planting, waiting or reaping? To fight the station is to suffer twice.

licoes.r: Sixth principle: every cause has an effect; chance is just an unknown law. Your choices today are tomorrow's crops.
licoes.a: Honesty: Karma, in Indian traditions, has various meanings and is not divine punishment; it is the law of action and its marks on the mind. That the universe returns every act is belief, not science. But taking ownership of one's choices is wisdom in any tradition. Heraclitus said: a man's character is his destiny. Practice: Before you make a decision today, ask yourself, what does this choice entail?
licoes.c: To contemplate: the Caibalion teaches to be cause and not effect, to move from within and not be moved by others. How many of your reactions today were choices, and how many were echoes?

licoes.r: Seventh principle: gender is in everything; everything has a male and a female principle. This is not about biological sex, but about two forces: the one that designs and the one that welcomes and generates.
licoes.a: Inner reading: creating requires both. Whoever only acts burns out; whoever only receives stagnates. Taoism says something similar to yin and yang, and Jung spoke of the anima and animus within each person. Practice: If today you only pushed, stop and listen; if you only waited, take a step.
licoes.c: To contemplate: all true creation is born of an inner marriage, between will and surrender. Which of these two forces is missing in you?

licoes.r: Quantum physics describes the world from the very small: atoms, electrons and light. It's one of the most tested theories in history, and from it came the laser, the transistor and the cell phone in your hand.
licoes.a: Deep reading: The most haunting is not what she promises, it's what she admits. Richard Feynman said in 1965: I think I can safely say that no one understands quantum mechanics. The theory works with absurd precision, but what it means, the so-called interpretations, are still up for debate. Honestly, a lot of what's sold as quantum healing, money and attraction has nothing to do with real physics. Practice: When you hear the word quantum in a product, ask, what's the experiment?
licoes.c: To contemplate: mankind's most accurate physics has ended in an open door to mystery. Let your certainty be like hers: firm in what is measured and humble in what is not yet known.

licoes.r: In quantum physics, measuring a system changes what you observe. But observer, here, is any physical interaction of measurement, like a detector. It doesn't have to be a human mind.
licoes.a: This is the point most distorted by mysticism. Whether consciousness has any role in measurement is an open and minority question among physicists. Werner Heisenberg wrote, in Physics and Philosophy, 1958, that what we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning. Inner reading: the way you ask defines what you can see. Practice: In a difficult conversation today, change the question of who's right to what I'm still not seeing.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the mystics speak of the witness, the consciousness that observes without interfering. Physics talks about measurement, which always interferes. Perhaps the wisdom is to learn to look without grasping.

licoes.r: In the double-slit experiment, electrons fired one by one form a wave pattern. If you measure which slit each one went through, the pattern disappears.
licoes.a: This shows that nature, at this scale, behaves neither like balls nor like ordinary waves. Feynman said that this experiment contains the only mystery of quantum physics. Inner reading: reality doesn't fit into our categories of this or that. Practice: Today, in front of someone you labeled, ask what that person is beyond the label.
licoes.c: To contemplate: before being measured, the electron has no defined path. How much of your life is still open, waiting for your choice to take shape?

licoes.r: Superposition is a system being in a combination of states until it is measured. Schrödinger's cat of 1935 was created precisely to show how absurd this seems on a human scale.
licoes.a: In large objects, interaction with the environment destroys the superposition very quickly; this is called decoherence. That's why you don't see live and dead cats at the same time. Inside reading: while you're undecided, all possibilities coexist, and indecision also comes at a price. Practice: Pick a small decision today that you've been putting off and make it.
licoes.c: For contemplation: Schrödinger, besides being a physicist, studied the Upanishads and wrote that consciousness is a singular whose plural is unknown. What about you is one, under so many roles?

licoes.r: Tangled particles have correlated outcomes, even at great distances. Einstein called it ghostly action at a distance. The experiments confirmed the phenomenon, and the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger for these tests.
licoes.a: Honesty: entanglement doesn't allow you to send messages faster than light, nor does it connect minds. Inside reading, as a metaphor and not as a physics: the universe is not made of isolated parts, and physicist David Bohm proposed an implicit order in which everything would be folded into the whole. It's an interpretation, not a consensus. Practice: think of someone far away today and make real contact.
licoes.c: To contemplate: separate is the way the eyes see. Whole is the way nature works at the bottom. Where do you live as if you were separated?

licoes.r: For modern physics, vacuum is nothing: it's full of quantum fields, with small fluctuations of energy. That's measurable, like the Casimir effect.
licoes.a: But the quantum field is not a field of wishful thinking where you make requests to the universe; here poetry and physics separate. Inside reading: The Tao Te Ching, in chapter eleven, says it's the emptiness of the vessel that makes it useful. Practice: leave a blank space in your calendar today, unfilled, and see what comes of it.
licoes.c: To contemplate: emptiness is not absence, it is power. What can only be born in you if you stop filling everything?

licoes.r: Heisenberg's 1927 Uncertainty Principle says that one cannot know, at the same time and with complete precision, the position and motion of a particle. It is not a failure of the instruments: it is a property of nature.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the universe has limits to certainty, and humility is a form of wisdom. Socrates said something similar in the Apology: he was wiser only because he knew he didn't know. Practice: today, say I don't know at least once, without shame.
licoes.c: To reflect: How much of your anxiety is a requirement for certainty in a world that does not offer it? Peace is not knowing everything, it's being right in the middle of what you don't know.

licoes.r: Some hypotheses, like that of Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff, suggest that consciousness involves quantum processes in the brain. It's a bold, unproven and highly contested hypothesis.
licoes.a: Most neuroscientists think the brain is too hot and humid to sustain delicate quantum effects. But the question remains open. Honest science says we don't know yet. Practice: when someone uses quantum consciousness to sell something, ask, what study, published where?
licoes.c: For contemplation: maybe consciousness doesn't need quantum to be a mystery. She's already the biggest of them. Tell the mystery of consciousness to go deeper.

licoes.r: Quantum mysticism is using words from physics to sell spiritual ideas. Be wary of quantum healing, quantum wealth and quantum devices.
licoes.a: You can have spirituality without pretending it's physical. Feynman taught in 1974: the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Truth needs no fantasy, and real science is haunting enough. Practice: separate, on a piece of paper, what you believe from experience and what you believe because someone sold you.
licoes.c: To reflect: Why do we want science to confirm faith? The inner experience has its own value; it doesn't need a vest. And science has its own value; it doesn't need incense.

licoes.r: Discipline is choosing what you want most instead of what you want now. Start small, every day, no negotiation.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the word comes from disciple, one who learns. Discipline is not punishment, it's loyalty to yourself. Rule of thumb: never miss two days in a row; one bad day is an accident, two have become a habit. Practice: set a nonnegotiable minimum, so small you can't get away from it, and meet it today.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Whose disciple are you today, his values or his impulses? Freedom is not doing what you want, it's being able to want what you choose.

licoes.r: Focus is saying no to almost everything. One task at a time, cell phone away, twenty-five minutes without interruption: that's the Pomodoro technique.
licoes.a: The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Where your attention goes, your life goes. Practice: Before you begin, write down the one thing you need to get ready, and work on it until the alarm goes off.
licoes.c: To reflect: Distraction is not just a cell phone problem, it's an escape from something. What are you running from when you pick up the phone for no reason?

licoes.r: Stoicism teaches you to separate what depends on you from what doesn't. Take care of the first. Accept the second.
licoes.a: Epitetus, who was born a slave, wrote in the Manual: It is not the things that disturb men, but the judgments they make about them. Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, wrote his Meditations for himself. Seneca reminded us that while we procrastinate, life passes. Practice: At night, like Seneca, review the day: what I did right, where I went wrong, what I'll do tomorrow.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the Stoics meditated on death, the memento mori, not out of sadness, but to give weight to the day. If today was your last day, what wouldn't matter?

licoes.r: Take a deep breath: four seconds to enter, four to hold, six to release. Repeat five times. If anxiety is frequent, seek medical attention.
licoes.a: Technique five, four, three, two, one: name five things you see, four you touch, three you hear, two you smell and one you taste. It brings the mind to the present. Inner reading: anxiety lives in the future; the body only exists now. If you're in distress, call 188, the CVV, free of charge, anytime.
licoes.c: For contemplation: Jesus said, in Matthew 6, never worry about tomorrow, for each day has enough trouble of its own. What is the one step you have to take today? Stay only with it. And remember, asking for help is strength.

p: what is the meaning of life
licoes.r: Purpose is not found ready; it is built. He lives where what you love meets what the world needs.
licoes.a: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived Auschwitz, quoted Nietzsche: "He who has a reason to live endures almost any way". In the book Pursuit of Meaning, he teaches that meaning is found in work, love, and the attitude toward suffering. Practice: ask, what problem bothers me so much that I would like to solve? And serve a little bit in that direction this week.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Frankl said that it is not we who ask life what its meaning is; it is life that asks us, every day. What is life asking you today?

licoes.r: Everything passes, the pain, the joy, the stages. To accept impermanence is to stop fighting the river.
licoes.a: In Buddhism, impermanence, anicca, is one of the three marks of existence.
