licoes.r: In the text, it is a command attributed to God through the prophet Samuel. 1 Samuel 15:3: strike Amalek and destroy it completely; you shall kill men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep. The reason given at 15:2 is what Amalek did to Israel centuries earlier at the exodus from Egypt. Saul loses his kingdom for not keeping his promises. Apologists' answer: Amalek was a recidivist aggressor people, and the total language is war hyperbole.
licoes.a: What the research says: this is one of the most difficult texts for Christian and Jewish theology itself. Rabbis over the centuries have restricted it to the point of making it inapplicable, and many theologians frankly say that it reflects the war mentality of the day, not the will of God as revealed in Jesus. Inner reading: the text punishes Saul for having spared; human conscience today punishes the opposite. That tension is the question the portal will answer.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Can a child bear the guilt of what his people did four hundred years ago?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.r: Here the text mixes two voices, and you have to separate them. Numbers 31:1-2: God tells Moses to avenge the sons of Israel of the Midianites. The harshest command comes from Moses, a human, in 31:15-18: kill all the boys and all the women who have known a man; but the virgin girls, let them live for yourselves. Apologists' answer: It was judgment by the seduction of Peor, and captives were taken as wives under laws that prohibited selling them, such as Deuteronomy 21:10-14.
licoes.a: What the research says: The text does not say that God commanded the killing of the boys; it is Moses who is indignant and gives the order, and the chapter goes on without reproach, counting at 31:35 thirty-two thousand virgin girls among the spoils. Many scholars read the chapter as a late, priestly composition with no historical confirmation. Even the law of Deuteronomy 21, which forbids the sale of the captive, presupposes a woman taken by force after the death of her family. Inner reading: Honesty is not softening the text nor attributing to God what the text attributes to Moses.
licoes.c: To contemplate: what happened to those girls? The Bible doesn't say. Silence is also a text.
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.t: The bears and the forty-two boys
p: the bears and the forty-two boys
licoes.r: 2 Kings 2:23-24: Some boys mocked Elisha, saying, "Go up, bald man!" And he cursed them in the name of Jehovah; and two bears came out of the woods, and tore forty-two of them to pieces. The text does not say that God sent the bears; it links the curse made in the name of the Lord to the attack. Apologists' answer: The Hebrew word translated boys, naar, can mean boys or young men, and mockery would be a threatening rejection of God's prophet.
licoes.a: What the research says: Elisha's stories form a cycle of prophetic legends that show the power of the man of God, and this serves as a warning: Don't mock the prophet. It is the exact same do not touch anointed one mechanism used today. Inside Reading: Jesus, when his disciples wanted to send fire from heaven upon a town that rejected him, rebuked them, as recorded at Luke 9:54-55. Within the Bible itself, one story corrects another.
licoes.c: To reflect: What fear is planted in a child when he hears that mocking a preacher brings divine punishment?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.r: In the text, it is God who acts. 2 Samuel 6:6-7: the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah stretched out his hand and took hold of the ark; and the anger of Jehovah was kindled, and God smote him there; and Uzzah died there by the ark. Apologists' answer: The law commanded that no one touch sacred things, lest he die, as at Numbers 4:15, and the ark was not even to be in an ox cart.
licoes.a: What the research says: The text itself records the human reaction, at 6:8-11: David was saddened, feared the Lord and left the ark in the house of Obed-Edom for three months. Many readers here see the ancient idea of the sacred as a dangerous, almost electric force that admits no contact. Inside reading: Uzzah wanted to protect the sacred and died; how many people today live in fear that a wrong gesture will condemn them?
licoes.c: To ponder: Does your God punish a good intention for a rule error? If so, who designed that God for you?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.t: Death by Stoning in the Law
p: death by stoning in the law
licoes.r: In the text, they are commands attributed to God. Numbers 15:32-36: A man who gathers wood on the sabbath, of whom Jehovah had said to Moses, shall surely be put to death; and all the congregation shall stone him. Deuteronomy 21:18-21: the stubborn and rebellious son, a glutton and a drunkard, brought by his parents to the elders, would be stoned to death. Apologists' Answer: They were civil laws of ancient Israel, which Jesus fulfilled and surpassed, and do not apply to Christians.
licoes.a: What the research says: The rabbis of the Talmud themselves, in their treatise Sanhedrin, surrounded the law of the prodigal son with so many conditions that they concluded: There has never been and never will be a prodigal son so condemned. Jewish tradition already read the Law with interpretation and mercy. Internal reading: a text is only dangerous when its context is ripped out and its interpretation removed. The death penalty for a disobedient son, uttered today from the pulpit as a threat, is manipulation.
licoes.c: To reflect: If rabbis already softened this law two thousand years ago, why would anyone today use their handwriting to scare a child?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.r: In the text, they are laws attributed to God. Leviticus 25:44-46: from the foreigners you shall buy male and female slaves; you shall leave them as an inheritance to your children, forever. Exodus 21:20-21: if a master strikes his servant with a rod and the servant survives a day or two, he shall not be punished, for the servant is his money. Apologists' Answer: Ancient slavery was different from modern slavery, the Law regulated it without approving it, and Exodus 21:16 punished by death anyone who kidnapped and sold a person.
licoes.a: What the research says: These verses were quoted by pastors and theologians in the United States and Brazil in defense of African slavery, and that is exactly why the Southern Baptist Convention was born in 1845. Christian abolitionists responded in the spirit of the Gospel, such as Galatians 3:28. Both sides quoted the Bible; what changed was the conscience. Internal reading: a text does not defend itself; one must ask who the reading serves.
licoes.c: To reflect: If the Bible was used to enslave and to set free, what determines the use - the text or the heart of the reader?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.t: Job and the Gamble with Satan
p: job and the gamble with satan
o senhor deu e o senhor tirou
licoes.r: In the text, the one who acts is Satan, but with God's permission. Job 1:12: the Lord said to Satan, all that he has is in your power; only do not lay a hand on him. At 1:18-19, a strong wind collapses the house and kills Job's sons and daughters. And Job answers, in 1:21: The Lord hath given, and the Lord hath taken away. The apologists' answer: the book does not explain suffering, it shows that faith can cross it, and in the end God answers Job from the whirlwind.
licoes.a: What the research says: Job is a work of wisdom, probably a poetic parable, not a chronicle. Its center is a protest: Job questions God for dozens of chapters, and at the end, in Job 42:7, God says to his accusing friends: You have not spoken about me what is upright, as my servant Job has. Inside reading: The oldest book on suffering defends the right to complain to God, and condemns religious who blame the victim.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Job's ten children died in a bet. Do you accept this story as it is, as a parable, or as fact? Every reading changes your God.
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: ordenadas ou feitas por Deus no texto

licoes.r: Here there is no command of God: the vow is of a man. Judges 11:30-31: Jephthah promises that the first one who comes out of his house to meet him will be a burnt offering. His only daughter comes out. At 11:39 he fulfilled in her the vow that he had made; and she had not known a man. Apologists' answer: Many, from medieval rabbis like David Kimchi, argue that she was consecrated to celibacy and not killed, and God never asked for this vow.
licoes.a: What the research says: Most scholars read the text as a real human sacrifice, narrated as the tragedy of a hasty vow. The text neither approves nor condemns him, and the Letter to the Hebrews, at 11:32, lists Jephthah among the heroes of faith. The daughter is unnamed; at 11:40 p.m., the daughters of Israel went yearly to mourn her for four days. Inside reading: How many religious promises, made in despair, have been paid for with the lives of those who promised nothing?
licoes.c: Consider: Jephthah's daughter is not named in the text. What name would you give her, and what would you say to her?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.r: Narrated as done by humans. Judges 19:25-29: To protect himself, the Levite hands over his concubine to the men of Gibeah, who molest her all night. In the morning she falls at the door with her hands on the threshold. He says, get up, let's go; she doesn't answer. At home, he cuts her into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel. Apologists' response: Judges describes, not approves; the book shows the moral collapse of a people without a king, as it repeats its end.
licoes.a: What the research says: Theologian Phyllis Trible called this and other accounts horror texts, and she called for them to be read in memory of the victims. The book closes at Judges 21:25: In those days there was no king in Israel; each one did what was right in his own eyes. The narrator criticizes anarchy; but the silence about the woman's pain is total. Inner reading: reading these texts is an act of memory; hiding them from the pulpit is choosing which victims deserve to be remembered.
licoes.c: To reflect: The Bible does not give this woman a voice. Reading her story to the end is one way to give her that voice back.
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.t: The War Against Benjamin and the Kidnapping of the Girls of Shiloh
p: the war against benjamin and the kidnapping of the girls of shiloh
licoes.r: Narrated as done by humans. After the crime of Gibeah, the tribes attack Benjamin; in Judges 20:28, they consult the Lord, who answers, "Come up". But what follows is the decision of the assembly: at 20:46-48, they kill men and animals and burn the cities; at 21:10-12, they have all in Jabesh-gilead killed, sparing four hundred virgins; and at 21:20-23, they have the Benjamites ambush and take away the dancing girls of Shiloh. Apologists' response: The book ends by showing, on purpose, how far a people without law and without king can go.
licoes.a: What the research says: Scholars read the end of Judges as a propaganda for monarchy: Without a king, everything would be chaos. To repair one massacre, the people commit another, and to restore women, they authorize a kidnapping. Honesty: The first battle has divine approval in the text; the extermination of Jabesh and the abduction of Shiloh are human decisions, and the text does not say that God commanded them. Inner reading: one unresolved violence breeds another, when no one has the courage to stop.
licoes.c: To reflect: Have you ever seen a community, or a family, trying to right a wrong with another wrong?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.r: Narrated as done by a human, and condemned by God in the text. 2 Samuel 11:14-15: David writes to Joab, places Uriah at the front where the fighting is fierce, and withdraws from him, so that he may be wounded and die, and sends the letter by the hand of Uriah himself. At 12:9, the prophet Nathan accuses: Uriah the Hittite you have killed with the sword, and his wife you have taken. Apologists' answer: The Bible does not hide the sin of its heroes, and Psalm 51 shows David's repentance.
licoes.a: What the research says: Many scholars and theologians point out that Bath-sheba, summoned by the most powerful king in the land, could hardly have refused, and that the text blames David, not her. Nathan is a rare role model: a religious man who confronts power and says, that man is you, at 12:7. Inside reading: The anointed David also erred, and the prophet did not keep quiet. This text is the best antidote against not touching the anointed one.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Who is Nathan in your life, the person who has the courage to tell you the truth?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.r: Narrated as done by a human. 2 Samuel 13:14: Amnon the son of David would not listen to the voice of Tamar his half sister, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her. Then he drove her out. At 13:21, when David learned of it, his anger was greatly kindled, but the text records no punishment of his son. Apologists' response: The text exposes sin and shows the tragic consequences in the house of David, as Nathan had foretold.
licoes.a: What the research says: Tamar is one of the few victims who speaks in the text: she argues, pleads, resists, and then tears her clothes and places ashes on her head in public. The father's silence, which does not punish, has been read by many theologians as the portrait of family cover-up. Inner reading: It is a text that many churches avoid; but for those who have suffered abuse, knowing that the Bible records Tamar's grief, and her father's omission, can be liberating.
licoes.c: To contemplate: Tamar was not silent. What does your community do when someone talks?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.r: Narrated as done by a human. Matthew 2:16: When Herod saw that he had been outwitted by the Magi, he became greatly enraged and sent out to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its environs who were two years old and under. Apologists' Answer: Bethlehem was small, perhaps twenty children, which would explain why historians of the time did not record the fact, and Herod even killed the children.
licoes.a: What the research says: The historian Flavius Josephus records many atrocities of Herod, but not this one, which is recorded only by Matthew. Many scholars read it as a narrative mirroring the Pharaoh of Exodus 1:22, presenting Jesus as a new Moses; others consider it plausible. Honest seal: tradition, without historical confirmation. Inside reading: the text denounces the power that kills children to protect itself, and that unfortunately has never ceased to be true.
licoes.c: To contemplate: What powers today sacrifice children to keep from losing their throne?
licoes.pa: Atrocidades: narradas como feitas por humanos

licoes.t: The Evolution of the Image of Jehovah
p: god s children in the nacoes
the evolution of the image of jehovah
licoes.r: Academic research shows that the image of God changes throughout the Bible. Deuteronomy 32:8-9 says in the Almeida: When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel; for the portion of the Lord is his people. But one of the Dead Sea Scrolls and the ancient Greek translation bring forth children of God, not of Israel. Apologists' Answer: The sons of God would be angels guarding the nations, under the one true God.
licoes.a: What the research says: Scholars such as Mark Smith and Thomas Römer, author of The Invention of God, read in this verse the memory of a time when the Most High, El, divided the nations among lesser gods, and Yahweh received Israel. Javé would have been a warrior and storm god coming from the south, then merged with El. Eighth-century B.C.E. inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai bless in the name of Yahweh and his Asherah, a sign that many Israelites worshipped a goddess besides Yahweh. Strict monotheism, one God and no other, took hold around the time of the Babylonian exile in the sixth century before Christ. Seal: What the manuscripts bring is proven; the reconstruction of Yahweh's story is a strong scholarly hypothesis. Inner reading: Israel's faith matured, and the Bible preserves the layers of that path.
licoes.c: To reflect: If God's image evolved within the Bible itself, can it continue to evolve within you?
licoes.pa: A outra face do Deus da Bíblia

p: o deus do antigo testamento e mau
licoes.r: About the year 144, Marcion, a wealthy Christian in Rome, taught that the righteous, warrior God of the Old Testament was not the loving Father announced by Jesus. He compiled the first Christian list of sacred books, without the Old Testament, and wrote the Antitheses, contrasting, for example, an eye for an eye from Exodus with the offering the other side of Matthew 5:38-39. Church Response: Marcion was declared a heretic, and the church affirmed that there is one God in both testaments.
licoes.a: What Gnostic tradition says: Texts found at Nag Hammadi speak of a demiurge, a lesser, ignorant creator, sometimes called Yaldabaoth, who claims to be the only god. That is Gnostic tradition, attributed to her, not fact. What is a historical fact is that Marcion's question of how the God of Joshua could be the Father of Jesus never ceased to be asked, and the reaction to it helped the Church to define its canon. Inner reading: Whoever asks this today is not the first; they are in a conversation almost two thousand years old.
licoes.c: To think about it: Have you also felt that the God you have been taught does not match the Jesus you read about? What do you do with that?
licoes.pa: A outra face do Deus da Bíblia

licoes.t: God is Love - Answers From Theology
p: how to reconcile the god of the old testament
god is love - answers from theology
como conciliar deus do antigo testamento
licoes.r: 1 John 4:8 says: "God is love". And Jesus, at Matthew 5:43-44, says: "You heard that it was said, 'You must hate your enemy; but I say to you, Love your enemies.' How do you reconcile that with the war texts? Theology offers many answers, and the Portal presents them all without choosing for you.
licoes.a: Key answers attributed to their proponents: Origen, in the third century, read violent texts as an allegory of spiritual struggle. Progressive revelation says that God revealed himself gradually, adapted to the mindset of each age, right down to Jesus. Paul Copan argues that the language of war is exaggeration typical of the ancient East. Gregory Boyd, in The Crucifixion of the Warrior God, 2017, argues that the cross is the lens, and that where the text contradicts the love of Christ, it reflects the authors' limited vision. Inside reading: all these answers came from people who took the problem seriously, not from those who hid it.
licoes.c: To ponder, which of these answers convinces you? And if none convinces, does that take away your faith or lead you to a more adult faith?
licoes.pa: A outra face do Deus da Bíblia

p: nao toqueis nos meus ungidos versiculo
licoes.r: Psalm 105:15: do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm. It's used to forbid any criticism of pastors and leaders. But verses 9 to 14 show who the psalm speaks of - Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who wandered from nation to nation, and God rebuked kings to protect them. The wearer's answer: The leader is anointed and can only be judged by God.
licoes.a: The context teaches the opposite of usage: the psalm protects frail people from powerful kings, not powerful ones from questions. In the Bible, the prophet Nathan confronts anointed King David, and Paul resists Peter in person at Galatians 2:11. Acts 17:11 commends those who examined the Scriptures to see if what Paul himself said was true. This use has a name: proof-texting, pulling a verse out of context to prove what you already wanted. How to protect yourself: Always read the entire psalm and ask who it speaks of. Inner reading: A leader who needs this verse not to be questioned has already answered the question.
licoes.c: For contemplation: Are you afraid to ask your leader a question? Where did that fear come from?

licoes.r: Malachi 3:10 Bring all the tithes into the treasury, and try me now, if I will not open unto you the windows of heaven. And 3:8-9: ye rob me in the tithes; ye are cursed with the curse. It's used to say that whoever doesn't tithe to the church is stealing from God and cursed. User's answer: The principle of honoring God with possessions still holds.
licoes.a: Context: The prophet speaks to the nation of Israel under the Mosaic Law some five hundred years before Christ. The tithe was in produce of the land, kept in the temple storehouse, so that there would be food in my house, and it sustained the Levites, who had no land; Nehemiah 13:10 shows the crisis when they did not receive. The New Testament does not command Christians to tithe; Paul, at 2 Corinthians 9:7, calls for a voluntary offering: each contributes as he has purposed in his heart; not with sorrow or under compulsion. How to protect yourself: Be suspicious of any promise of financial return in exchange for an offer, and hold the church accountable. Inner reading: Giving can be a beautiful act; giving out of fear of cursing is an imposed exchange.
licoes.c: To reflect: If you stopped giving for a month, of what would you be afraid? Is that fear of God or who taught it to you?

p: the wife must be subject to her husband
a mulher deve obedecer ao marido
licoes.r: Ephesians 5:22: Wives, be in subjection to your own husbands as to the Lord. It's used to keep women in abusive marriages. But the preceding verse, 5:21, says: "Be in subjection to one another in fear of Christ"; and 5:25 commands: "Husbands, continue loving your wives, just as the Christ also loved the congregation and delivered up himself for it". Answer: It is God's arrangement for the family, and the husband is the head.
licoes.a: The context: Paul writes within the Roman domestic code, in which the husband had almost total power, and he transforms it: Submission is mutual, and the pattern of the husband is to surrender, not dominate. No verse commands a woman to accept violence. Theologians of all stripes, including conservatives, claim that abuse breaks the covenant. How to protect yourself: In the event of violence, call 180, the Women's Health Center, or 190; no religion asks that you accept to be hurt. Inner reading: A verse quoted without neighbors becomes a chain; read whole, it is a limit against power.
licoes.c: For reflection, have you ever been silenced by someone using a scripture? What verse came just before or just after?

licoes.t: Servants, obey - the Bible of the slave masters
p: servants, obey - the bible of the slave masters
licoes.r: Ephesians 6:5: Slaves, obey those who are your masters according to the flesh with fear and trembling. Colossians 3:22 repeats: be obedient in all things. And Genesis 9:25, cursed be Canaan, servant of servants, was read, without reference to the text, as the curse of Ham and the Africans. These verses sustained sermons to enslaved people in the Americas. The wearer's answer: Slavery was a divine order and obedience a Christian virtue.
licoes.a: What is proven: There was a Slave Bible, published in London in 1807 for use in the colonies, which cut out most of the Exodus and passages that spoke of freedom. Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, and it does not mention color or Africa. And Paul, at Galatians 3:28, says: There is neither slave nor free; you are all one in Christ Jesus. How to protect yourself: When a scripture is used to say that a group was born to serve, read the entire chapter and the story of who used it. Inner reading: the one who has power chooses the verses; the one who wants freedom reads the whole book.
licoes.c: To reflect: If someone had to cut out Exodus from the Bible to control people, what does that say about the liberating power of the entire text?

licoes.r: Romans 13:1-2: Let every soul be in subjection to the superior authorities, for there is no authority except that which comes from God; the one who opposes the authority has taken a stand against the arrangement of God. It was used to support the Nazi regime, apartheid in South Africa and dictatorships, including in Latin America. User's Answer: Order and government are God's institutions, and the Christian must obey.
licoes.a: Background: Paul was writing to a small community in Rome that needed to escape persecution. The text itself says, at 13:3, that magistrates are a cause for fear, not to those doing good, but to those doing bad. And at Acts 5:29, Peter and the apostles, arrested for preaching, answer: We must obey God as ruler rather than men. Christians like Dietrich Bonhoeffer, executed in 1945, resisted Nazism because of their faith. How to protect yourself: Civil obedience is different from obedience to injustice; your conscience remains yours. Inside reading: Anyone who uses Romans 13 to silence their conscience forgets that the Bible is full of prophets who disobeyed unjust kings.
licoes.c: To ponder: Is there a limit to obedience? Where's yours?

licoes.t: Obey your guides and the discipline of the church
p: obey your guides and the discipline of the church
licoes.r: Hebrews 13:17: Obey those who are taking the lead among you, being in subjection to them. And Matthew 18:17: if he refuses to listen to the church, treat him as a Gentile and a publican. They are used to demand total obedience to leaders and to isolate anyone who asks or leaves, severing friendships and even family ties. Answer: The church has spiritual authority and must correct to protect the flock.
licoes.a: Context: Hebrews speaks of guides who watch over souls and will render an account, not of conscience holders. Matthew 18 describes a way of reconciliation between brothers for a real sin, alone first, and Jesus was rightly criticized for eating with publicans and sinners, as at Matthew 9:11. The Bible also commands: "Test everything out", at 1 Thessalonians 5:21. How to protect yourself: Keep your ties out of the group, and be wary of any community that forbids you from talking to your outsider. Internal reading: a reconciliation text used as an exclusion weapon is one of the hallmarks of group control that the Portal describes in Pandora's Box.
licoes.c: To contemplate: treating someone like a publican, for Jesus, was to sit at the table with him. How does your community treat those who leave?

licoes.t: Revelation 21:8 and the Fear of Hell
p: the cowards will go to hell
the disbelievers will be in hell
revelation 21 8 and the fear of hell
os medrosos irao para o inferno
licoes.r: Rev. 21:8 But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, and all liars - their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death. It's used to terrorize those who doubt or want to leave the church. User response: Hell is real, and warning is an act of love.
licoes.a: Context: The Apocalypse is an apocalyptic text, full of symbols, written for churches persecuted by the Roman Empire; the cowardly are those who denied the faith out of fear of persecution, not those who have sincere doubts. Christians have different readings of hell: eternal torment, annihilation, the hope of universal salvation; it is tradition and interpretation, not proven fact. How to protect yourself: Read the entire book of Revelation with a historical introduction, and note that it ends with the healing of the nations in chapter 22. Inner reading: A child terrified by the lake of fire has not learned the love of God; he has learned fear.
licoes.c: To ponder, was your faith born of love or fear of burning? Which one would make you a better person?

p: every word of the bible and of god
cada palavra da biblia e de deus
licoes.r: 2 Timothy 3:16: All Scripture is divinely inspired and beneficial for teaching, for reproving, for setting things straight, for disciplining in righteousness. It is used to say that every word of a modern translation is dictated by God, and that any question is rebellion. User's answer: If the Bible is inspired, it cannot be in error at all.
licoes.a: The context: When the letter was written, the New Testament as a book did not yet exist; the Scriptures were the Hebrew Bible, the sacred letters that Timothy had known since infancy, as verse 15 says. The text says what Scripture is for, teaching and correcting, not the absence of copying errors. The church itself acknowledges copying errors, such as Ahaziah's age. Inspiration is a statement of faith; inerrancy of a translation is a statement that the manuscripts disprove. How to protect yourself: Compare two or three translations and consult the footnotes of a study Bible. Inner reading: Those who love the text want to know it as it is.
licoes.c: To think about it, does your faith stand up to knowing that the Bible has history, copyists, and translations? If she holds out, she gets stronger.

licoes.t: The whole Bible is more than loose verses
p: the whole bible is more than loose verses
licoes.r: After seeing contradictions, atrocities and verses used to manipulate, the Portal's conclusion is not to throw the Bible away, nor to pretend none of that is there. It's reading the whole book, with context, with history and with questions. Acts 17:11 commends the Beroeans, who examined the Scriptures daily as to whether these things were so, including what the apostle was saying. And 1 Thessalonians 5:21 sums it up: Make sure of all things; hold fast to what is fine.
licoes.a: How to do it: Read an entire book at once, like a letter. Ask who wrote, to whom, when and why. Compare translations, and when you can, consult a scholarly study Bible. Separate what the text says God did, what it says humans did, and what interpreters say today. And look who profits from the reading they taught you. Inner reading: Manipulators rely on loose verses; the entire Bible, with all its voices, is too large to fit in someone's hand.
licoes.c: To think about it: Reading the Bible as a whole and in context releases more than loose verses. Which book of hers are you going to read in its entirety this week?

licoes.t: Who created the Trinity: the timeline
p: father son and holy spirit origin
origin of the father son and holy spirit
who created the trinity the timeline
pai filho e espirito santo origem
origem do pai filho e espirito santo
licoes.r: The Trinity was not created by one person, nor in a single day. It was formulated over some three hundred years. The New Testament already has formulas with three names, such as baptizing in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in Matthew 28:19, but it does not explain the doctrine. The word Trinity appears around 180, with Theophilus of Antioch, and in Latin, Trinitas, around 213, with Tertullian. The official definitions came in two councils: Nicaea, in 325, about the Son, and Constantinople, in 381, about the Holy Spirit.
licoes.a: The timeline: around 55, Paul writes the blessing of the grace of Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, in 2 Corinthians 13:14, which in some Bibles is 13:13. Around 100, the Didache, an early Christian manual, repeats the baptism formula in three names. Around 112, the Roman governor Pliny the Younger tells the emperor that Christians sang hymns to Christ as to a god. Around 213, Tertullian writes Against Praxeas and speaks of one substance and three persons. In the third century, Origen uses the word hypostasis, but places the Son below the Father. Around 318, the priest Arius says the Son was created, and the great dispute begins. In 325, Nicaea declares the Son of the same substance as the Father, but about the Spirit it says only: and in the Holy Spirit. Between 360 and 380, the Cappadocian Fathers, Basil and the two Gregories, establish the formula of one essence and three persons. In 381, Constantinople completes the creed about the Spirit. Then come the Athanasian Creed, written in Latin in the fifth or sixth century, and not by Athanasius; and the Filioque, the phrase and the Son, added in the West from 589 onward and one of the reasons for the split between Rome and the East, in 1054. The theologians' answer: the doctrine was not invented; it was a way of explaining what the first Christians already lived when they worshipped the Father, the Son and the Spirit. Practice: when you hear that something was always this way, ask when it was written, by whom and in the middle of which dispute.
licoes.c: To contemplate: an idea that took three hundred years and many councils to be defined, is it a finished revelation, or the human search to explain the mystery? Both answers can fit in the same faith; what does not fit is pretending there was no history.
s: Is the Trinity in the Bible?

licoes.t: Is the Trinity in the Bible?
p: is the trinity in the bible
does the bible talk about the trinity
the trinity is not in the bible
licoes.r: The word Trinity does not appear anywhere in the Bible, and neither does the phrase three persons and one essence. That is a fact. What exists are texts that speak of the Father, the Son and the Spirit together, and texts that call Jesus God, such as John 1:1 and John 20:28. There are also texts that seem to place the Son below the Father, such as John 14:28: the Father is greater than I.
licoes.a: How each side reads it: defenders of the Trinity say the doctrine gathers the pieces scattered through the Bible, like someone putting together a puzzle. Critics say the pieces were fitted with tools from Greek philosophy, such as the words essence and person, which the biblical authors did not use. Another text often cited by critics is Mark 13:32, where Jesus says that not even the Son knows the day of the end, only the Father. Throughout history, many sincere Christians did not accept the Trinity: the Arians in the fourth century; Michael Servetus, burned in Geneva in 1553 for denying the Trinity; the Unitarians; and today Jehovah's Witnesses and Oneness Pentecostals, each with their own reading. In other words, doubt about the Trinity is old within Christianity itself. The theologians' answer: not every truth of faith needs a technical word in the Bible; the word came later to protect what was believed. Practice: read John 1, John 14 and Mark 13 in full and write down what the text says, before what you were told it says.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if sincere Christians have disagreed about this for seventeen centuries, what does that say about those who claim that doubting the Trinity means certain damnation?
s: Who created the Trinity: the timeline
1 John 5:7: the Trinity verse that was added

p: the trinity was created by constantine
licoes.r: Myth. Constantine did not create the Trinity. The word Trinity is more than a hundred years older than him. At Nicaea, in 325, which he convened, the question was whether the Son was of the same substance as the Father; the Holy Spirit was barely discussed. The part of the creed about the Spirit was only defined in 381, in Constantinople, under the emperor Theodosius, forty-four years after Constantine's death.
licoes.a: What Constantine really did: he legalized Christianity in 313, convened and pressured the Council of Nicaea to end the dispute that divided the empire, and exiled those who did not sign. But later he changed sides: he called Arius back, exiled Athanasius, the greatest defender of Nicaea, in 335, and was baptized on his deathbed, in 337, by Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian bishop. His son, Constantius the Second, supported the Arians. In other words, Constantine's family helped the side that denied the equality of the Son more than the side of the Trinity. What is true in this suspicion: imperial power entered theology, and from then on disagreeing with the official doctrine could cost exile, and later life itself. In 380, Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion and called the others heretics. The theologians' answer: the council only put into words a faith that already existed, and the emperor did not decide the content. Practice: always separate two questions: who invented an idea, and who used power to impose it.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the myth that an emperor invented everything is simpler than the truth, and the truth is more serious: faith was married to the sword. What changes in you when you know this?

licoes.r: Triads of gods exist in many cultures, and that is real. In Egypt, Osiris, Isis and Horus form a family: father, mother and son. In Rome, Jupiter, Juno and Minerva were the Capitoline Triad. In India, the Trimurti unites Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. But the idea that the Christian Trinity is a direct copy of one of them is not accepted by most historians. Pagan triads are almost always three different gods; the Trinity says one God in three persons, and it was born among Jews who swore there was only one God.
licoes.a: What is a real parallel: the number three is sacred in almost every culture, and the psychologist Carl Jung saw an archetype in triads. An Egyptian hymn from Leiden, from around 1213 before Christ, says that all the gods are three, Amun, Ra and Ptah, and that the three are one; it is the closest parallel. In philosophy, Philo of Alexandria, a Jew of the first century, called the Logos, the Word, a second God; and Plotinus, who lived from 204 to 270, taught three principles: the One, the Intellect and the Soul. This Greek vocabulary influenced Christian theologians; that is accepted by research. What does not hold up: the Trimurti was organized in the Purana texts, from the fourth century after Christ onward, so it could not be the source; and the famous Babylonian trinity of Nimrod, Semiramis and Tammuz comes from the book The Two Babylons, by Alexander Hislop, from 1853, full of errors; the pastor Ralph Woodrow, who had written a book based on it, later refuted it and withdrew his own book. The theologians' answer: similarity of language is not copying; Christians used Greek words to explain a Jewish experience. Practice: when faced with a parallel, ask who came first, whether there is a document linking the two, and whether the similarity is of form or of content.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if all of humanity draws the sacred in threes, perhaps that says something about the human mind, and not about who copied whom. The truth does not need plagiarism to be questioned, nor originality to be lived.

licoes.t: 1 John 5:7: the Trinity verse that was added
p: three that bear record in heaven
the father the word and the holy ghost and these three are one
1 john 5 7 the trinity verse that was added
o pai a palavra e o espirito santo e estes tres sao um
licoes.r: The only verse in the Bible that says almost in so many words that the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit are one is 1 John 5:7. And it was added. The phrase about the three that bear record in heaven does not appear in any ancient Greek manuscript; the oldest one that has it is from the fourteenth century. That is why modern translations such as the NIV leave this passage out, or only mention it in a footnote. The King James Version still keeps it.
licoes.a: The history: the phrase first appears in Latin texts, around 380, linked to the bishop Priscillian, and probably began as a comment in the margin that later entered the text. Erasmus did not include it in the first two editions of his Greek New Testament, was accused of favoring the Arians, and included it in the third, in 1522, after a Greek manuscript containing it turned up, probably made to order at that time. That is how it entered the Textus Receptus and the old Bibles. Isaac Newton wrote a study of this alteration in 1690, published only after his death. In 1897, Rome forbade questioning the verse; in 1927, it reversed course and allowed research. Today Catholics, Protestants and secular scholars agree: it is not original. The theologians' answer: the Trinity does not depend on this verse; it was defined without it. Practice: open 1 John 5:7 and 8 in two translations, the King James Version and the NIV, and compare with your own eyes.
licoes.c: To contemplate: someone thought the truth needed a little help and wrote into the Bible what they wanted to read in it. How many of your certainties were also written in the margin by someone else?
s: Is the Trinity in the Bible?

licoes.t: The sin against the Holy Spirit and the fear of not being forgiven
p: i sinned against the holy spirit
did i sin against the holy spirit
the sin against the holy spirit and the fear of not being forgiven
sera que pequei contra o espirito santo
licoes.r: Jesus says in Matthew 12:31 and 32, and in Mark 3:28 and 29, that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. Hebrews 6:4 to 6 speaks of those who fell away and cannot be renewed. These verses are used to instill fear: if you doubt, leave the church or think something bad, you may have committed the sin of no return. Psychology knows this fear well: it is called scrupulosity, a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder with a religious theme, and it can be treated.
licoes.a: The context: in Mark 3:30, the text explains why Jesus said it: because they said he had an unclean spirit, that is, they called good evil. It was not about a thought that slips out, nor about a sincere doubt. The philosopher Bertrand Russell, in Why I Am Not a Christian, from 1927, said this verse caused an unspeakable amount of misery in the world, because many people came to believe they had committed it. A famous example is John Bunyan, author of The Pilgrim's Progress, who tells of living tormented by this fear for years. The research: a 2006 study from the Mayo Clinic, with OCD patients, linked scrupulosity to the belief that thoughts must be controlled and to thought-action fusion, the idea that thinking something bad is as serious as doing it. The most studied treatment is cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention, which has been adapted even for very religious people. The theologians' answer: most pastors and priests say that anyone afraid of having committed this sin shows precisely that they have not, because they still care about God; the Catholic Catechism defines it as refusing mercy forever. Practice: if a religious thought traps you in cycles of fear, guilt and rituals to find relief, this has a name and it can be treated; see a psychologist.
licoes.c: To contemplate: a text about not calling good evil became a weapon to call doubt a crime. Who profits when you are afraid to think?
s: Fear as a Tool of Control
Phobia indoctrination: fear of hell as a leash

licoes.t: Where the hell of fire came from
p: is hell in the hebrew bible
where the hell of fire came from
licoes.r: The hell of eternal fire is not in the Hebrew Bible. Sheol was the dark place of all the dead, good and bad, without torture. The idea of eternal punishment formed gradually: it appears faintly in Daniel 12:2, around 165 before Christ, and grows in the Jewish apocalyptic books, such as First Enoch, between the third and first centuries before Christ. In the New Testament, Jesus speaks of Gehenna, the name of the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem, where according to Jeremiah 7:31 children had been burned in sacrifice.
licoes.a: The influences: many scholars see Persian influence, because Zoroastrianism already had a final judgment, a bridge of the dead and a place of punishment, and the Jews lived under the Persians between 539 and 332 before Christ; this is a debated hypothesis, not a settled fact. The Greek influence is clearer: Hades and Tartarus, the prison of the Titans; 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb that means to cast into Tartarus. A common myth: that Gehenna was a garbage dump that was always burning. That explanation only appears around 1200, with the rabbi David Kimhi, and archaeology does not confirm it. Then came imagination: the Apocalypse of Peter, from the second century, describes detailed tortures; Augustine, in the fifth century, defends eternal and literal fire; Dante, between 1308 and 1321, draws hell in nine circles; and the preacher Jonathan Edwards, in 1741, in the sermon Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, compares the listener to a spider held over the fire. The theologians' answer: revelation is progressive, and Jesus would have revealed what was hidden before. Practice: when you imagine hell, ask where each image comes from: from the Bible, from Dante, or from a sermon.
licoes.c: To contemplate: the hell that frightens you has the face of which century? Much of what people fear is not in the text; it is in the painting someone made of it.
s: Phobia indoctrination: fear of hell as a leash
Infinite punishment for a finite mistake?

licoes.t: Infinite punishment for a finite mistake?
p: infinite punishment for a finite mistake
licoes.r: This is the so-called problem of hell, debated for centuries by philosophers, including Christians. The argument: a human life is short and limited, so no mistake in it could deserve endless suffering. The philosopher David Hume asked, in an essay published in 1777: why then eternal punishment for the temporary offences of so frail a creature as man? A punishment should be proportionate to the offense.
licoes.a: More voices: Hume also pointed out that a punishment without purpose, when it can no longer correct or protect anyone, does not fit our idea of goodness. Bertrand Russell called the doctrine of hell fire a doctrine of cruelty. The Christian philosopher Marilyn McCord Adams, in 1993, said that a God who created people knowing they would suffer forever would not be good to them. The Christian philosopher Thomas Talbott, in 1999, in the book The Inescapable Love of God, argues that God's love ends up winning everyone over. The classic answers: Augustine, in The City of God, defended eternal punishment against those he called the merciful ones. Anselm and Thomas Aquinas argued that the gravity of an offense depends on the dignity of the one offended, and offending an infinite God would be an infinite offense. C. S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain, from 1940, said that the damned are, in a sense, rebels to the end, and that the doors of hell are locked on the inside: God would not imprison anyone; the person would refuse to leave. The critics reply: in no just court is punishment ever measured by the dignity of the victim, and a child, or someone who never heard of God, does not choose hell with full awareness. Practice: read one argument from each side and notice which one requires you to switch off your sense of justice.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if a human father burned his son forever for one mistake, no one would call him just. Why would we accept from God a moral standard worse than our own? And, with respect for those who believe: what if your conscience, which revolts against this, is the best of God in you?
s: Eternal hell is not the only Christian reading
Would a God of love be an executioner?

licoes.t: Eternal hell is not the only Christian reading
p: eternal hell is not the only reading
eternal hell is not the only christian reading
inferno eterno nao e a unica leitura
licoes.r: Many people do not know it, but eternal torment was never the only Christian reading. There are three main positions. The first, eternal torment, is the most common in Catholicism and Protestantism. The second, annihilationism or conditional immortality, says that those who reject God cease to exist; it was defended, cautiously, by the Anglican pastor John Stott, in 1988. The third, universalism, says that in the end everyone will be reconciled with God.
licoes.a: Universalism has ancient roots: Origen, in the third century, and Gregory of Nyssa, in the fourth century, one of the very Fathers who defined the Trinity, hoped for the restoration of all, the apokatastasis. Isaac of Nineveh, in the seventh century, said that hell is the love of God felt as torment by those who refuse it. In 2019, the Orthodox theologian David Bentley Hart published That All Shall Be Saved, arguing that the Greek word translated as eternal, aionios, means of an age, and not necessarily without end. The official Catholic position, in the Catechism, affirms hell and its eternity, but Pope John Paul the Second, in 1999, explained that hell is not a punishment imposed externally by God, but the state of those who freely separate themselves from him, more a state than a place. The Catholic theologian Hans Urs von Balthasar argued that it is legitimate to hope that hell is empty. The Orthodox also vary. The answer of those who defend eternal torment: Matthew 25:46 puts eternal punishment beside eternal life, and if one is endless, the other would be too. Practice: if you were taught that there is only one reading, know that people of faith, holy and learned, thought differently.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if even the saints disagreed about hell, is the one who threatens you with it as absolute certainty speaking for God, or for themselves?
s: Infinite punishment for a finite mistake?
Would a God of love be an executioner?

licoes.t: Phobia indoctrination: fear of hell as a leash
p: phobia indoctrination fear of hell as a leash
licoes.r: Fear is one of the most studied tools of control. The cult expert Steven Hassan created the BITE model, which looks at four kinds of control: of behavior, of information, of thought and of emotions. Within emotional control is what he calls phobia indoctrination: implanting fears so strong that the person cannot even imagine leaving the group, such as going to hell, losing salvation or being destroyed. This can happen in any group; it is not an attack on anyone's faith.
licoes.a: What the research shows: in 2014, the psychologists Azim Shariff and Lara Aknin, in three studies, found that believing in heaven is linked to more happiness, while believing in hell is linked to less happiness and less life satisfaction; and just thinking about hell already worsened mood. Honesty: a 2012 study, by the same Shariff, found that countries where more people believe in hell have fewer crimes. In other words, fear works to control behavior; that is exactly why it is used, and it does not prove that hell exists. As early as 1777, Hume wrote that the terrors about the afterlife would soon vanish if they were not fostered by education, and asked what motive those who foster them have. The psychiatrist Robert Lifton called the dispensing of existence the idea that those outside the group do not deserve to exist. The theologians' answer: warning of a real danger is love, not manipulation; the problem is when the warning becomes a threat to obey the leader. Practice: when you feel religious fear, ask: who told me this, what do they gain if I obey, and can I verify it?
licoes.c: To contemplate: a fear that cannot be verified, but that forces you to obey someone who can, is it faith or a leash? The faith that sets free does not need bars.
s: Fear as a Tool of Control

licoes.t: Would a God of love be an executioner?
p: would a god of love be an executioner
how can god send people to hell
if god is love why is there hell
como deus pode mandar para o inferno
se deus e amor por que existe inferno
o perfeito amor lanca fora o medo
licoes.r: This is the most important question, and the Bible itself provides material for it. 1 John 4:18 says: there is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear. Ezekiel 18:23 and 32 says that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that he turn and live. 1 Timothy 2:4 says that God wants all people to be saved. A being who gives life and then tortures forever those who went wrong does not match this portrait.
licoes.a: Adding up the pieces: a loving father does not burn his son; a just judge gives a proportionate sentence; a doctor does not punish forever the patient who did not get well. Lamentations 3:31 to 33 says that the Lord does not cast off forever and does not willingly afflict. In the parable of the prodigal son, in Luke 15:20, the father runs to meet his son even before he asks for forgiveness. And 1 Corinthians 15:28 speaks of God being all in all. That is why many Christians conclude that the image of a torturing God comes more from human fear and religious power than from the love Jesus preached. The answer of theologians who defend hell: love also means respecting freedom; God forces no one to love him, and hell would be the person's final choice, not God's revenge. The critics reply: a choice made without full knowledge, out of fear, out of trauma or because of being born into another religion, is not truly a free choice. No one can prove what exists after death; that is unknown. Practice: read the whole of 1 John 4 and ask whether the God you were taught fits in it.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if you, with all your flaws, could not torture even your worst enemy forever, your heart has already answered the question. Perhaps God is greater than the fear you were taught about him.
s: Infinite punishment for a finite mistake?
God is Love - Answers From Theology

licoes.t: The final sum: truth, myth and manipulation
p: what is true about the trinity
what is a lie about hell
the final sum truth, myth and manipulation
o que e verdade sobre a trindade
o que e mentira sobre o inferno
o que e manipulacao na religiao
licoes.r: Adding it all up. It is proven truth: the word Trinity is not in the Bible; the doctrine was formulated between the second and fourth centuries, with Tertullian, Nicaea, in 325, and Constantinople, in 381; 1 John 5:7 was added; the hell of fire does not exist in the Hebrew Bible and took shape over time. It is myth: that Constantine invented the Trinity, and that it is a direct copy of a pagan trinity. It is manipulation: using the fear of hell and of the unforgivable sin to prevent questions and ensure obedience.
licoes.a: More details of the sum. Proven: the images of hell were expanded by Dante, in 1321, and by sermons like that of Jonathan Edwards, in 1741; and believing in hell is linked to lower well-being. Hypothesis: the Persian influence on the final judgment and the influence of Greek philosophy on the vocabulary of the Trinity; the second is widely accepted, the first is debated. Tradition: the Trinity, eternal hell, annihilation and the salvation of all are beliefs of faith; sincere Christians have defended each of them. Unknown: what exists after death; no one can prove hell, nor prove that it does not exist. Where the suspicion is right: the doctrine has a human history, it was backed by the power of the empire, and the fear of hell is used to control. Where history corrects: the Trinity was not born from Constantine nor from plagiarism; it was born from debates among Christians trying to explain their faith. The theologians' answer: that the doctrine has a history does not prove it is false; many truths were discovered little by little. Practice: keep this sum and use the same method for any belief: what is document, what is assumption, what is faith and what is fear.
licoes.c: To contemplate: freeing yourself from fear does not require hating anyone's faith. It only requires knowing how to separate what is history, what is mystery and what is a leash. What, in this sum, changed inside you?
s: Fear as a Tool of Control
Who created the Trinity: the timeline

p: how to lose the fear of hell
how to overcome the fear of hell
i can t stop being afraid of hell
como perder o medo do inferno
como superar o medo do inferno
medo de ir para o inferno
nao consigo parar de ter medo do inferno
licoes.r: Leaving the fear of hell behind does not happen all at once, and it does not have to be done with anger. The fear was learned, often in childhood, and the brain learns again with time and repetition. Three paths help: understanding the history, as in these lessons; caring for body and mind, with a psychologist; and replacing the voice of punishment with a voice of kindness toward yourself.
licoes.a: What the research supports: self-compassion, studied by the psychologist Kristin Neff, is treating yourself the way you would treat a dear friend who is suffering. A 2012 meta-analysis, by MacBeth and Gumley, brought together fourteen studies and found a strong link between more self-compassion and less anxiety, depression and stress; it is a link, not proof of cause. For those who live in cycles of obsessive religious thoughts, therapy with exposure and response prevention is the most studied treatment. Care: look for a licensed psychologist, whose registration you can check with the professional board (in Brazil, the Federal Council of Psychology), and who respects your faith or your lack of it. You do not need to abandon your faith to leave fear behind; many people find a faith based on love. If the suffering becomes too heavy, in Brazil call one eight eight, the CVV, free, at any time; in other countries, call your local crisis line. The theologians' answer: many pastors and priests also condemn preaching through terror and recall Matthew 11:28 to 30: come to me, and I will give you rest. Practice: when the fear of hell comes, breathe deeply three times, put your hand on your chest and say: this is a fear I was taught; I can look at it calmly.
licoes.c: To contemplate: fear taught you that you had to earn not being burned. What if the truth is simpler: that you deserve peace just for existing?
s: The sin against the Holy Spirit and the fear of not being forgiven
Phobia indoctrination: fear of hell as a leash

licoes.t: The Bible fell from the sky ready
p: the bible fell from the sky
the bible fell from the sky ready
the bible was written by god
a biblia foi escrita por deus
licoes.r: Myth. The Bible is a collection of dozens of books written by many authors in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek over a period of about a thousand years. The list of books, the canon, was gradually defined: Athanasius listed the 27 books of the New Testament in 367, and Catholics and Protestants to this day have different lists in the Old Testament.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Saying that a text is inspired is an affirmation of faith, and that is for each person to decide. To say that he fell straight from the sky is a historical claim, and the facts disprove it. Knowing how the Bible was formed does not take away its spiritual value; it takes away the power of the one who says he alone can read. Practice: Read an entire Bible book from cover to cover, asking who wrote it, to whom, and when.
licoes.c: To ponder: Does your faith depend on a book without history, or can it live up to the truth about how it was made?

p: constantine chose the books of the bible
o concilio de niceia escolheu os livros
constantino escolheu os livros da biblia
licoes.r: A myth, much repeated by critics of religion and popularized by the book The Da Vinci Code. The Council of Nicaea in 325 discussed the dispute with Arius over the nature of Christ, the date of Easter, and norms for the clergy. None of the ancient records and accounts speak of choosing the books of the Bible.
licoes.a: Inside reading: an anti-religious myth remains a myth. Anyone who wants out of the Matrix can't trade an unproven belief for another unproven belief. The real story is even more interesting: the canon has been forming for centuries, in debates between communities. Practice: whenever you hear a shocking revelation, ask: What is the document?
licoes.c: To reflect: Do you more readily accept lies that confirm what you already believe?

p: millions of dead in the inquisition
licoes.r: Myth. The figure of nine million witches emerged in the eighteenth century, in an unfounded extrapolation, and was repeated for centuries. Historical research estimates that between 40,000 and 60,000 were executed for witchcraft in Europe between 1450 and 1750, mostly by secular and local Catholic and Protestant courts. The Spanish, Portuguese and Roman Inquisitions combined executed a few thousand, not millions.
licoes.a: Inside reading: decreasing crime is lying, and inflating it is lying. Forty thousand people, most of them women, killed by fear and superstition, is already an immense tragedy; it needs no exaggeration to teach. Calculated truth protects against both sides. Practice: When a number seems too big, look for its academic source.
licoes.c: To reflect: Why does an exaggeration seem stronger than the truth? And what do we lose when we overdo it?

p: quantum physics proves the law of attraction
quantum mechanics and the law of attraction
fisica quantica prova a lei da atracao
a fisica quantica prova a manifestacao
mecanica quantica e lei da atracao
licoes.r: Myth. In physics, the observer is any interaction that records a measurement, like a detector, and not the human mind or desire. No experiment has shown that thoughts change material reality. Using words like quantum, frequency and vibration to sell manifestation is called quantum mysticism.
licoes.a: Inner reading: co-creation, as traditions teach, is an inner practice: intention, emotion and action aligned. She doesn't need a fake physique to be valuable, and she's more honest without it. Practice: When someone uses the word quantum to sell something, ask what experiment shows that.
licoes.c: To reflect: Why look to science for a guarantee for what only practice can confirm?

p: insanity and do the same thing
insanidade e fazer a mesma coisa
licoes.r: A common myth. The phrase insanity is doing the same thing and expecting different results does not appear in anything Einstein wrote; the earliest known occurrence is from a 1981 text by Narcotics Anonymous. Many other spiritual phrases attributed to Einstein also have no source. An actual quote from him, in a letter to Max Born in 1926: God doesn't throw dice, which he used to criticize quantum physics.
licoes.a: Inner reading: Putting a famous name in a sentence is a form of authority that dispenses with thought, the same mechanism of not touching the anointed. A good idea is worth it; a bad idea doesn't get better with a famous name. Practice: Before sharing a quote, look it up on Wikiquote or Quote Investigator.
licoes.c: To ponder: Would you agree with the sentence if it had no name underneath it?

licoes.r: A common myth. The phrase if you want to discover the secrets of the universe, think in terms of energy, frequency and vibration doesn't appear in any of Tesla's writings. Wikiquote classifies it as disputed: there is only the account of a third, Ralph Bergstresser, who said he heard it. There is also no source for the phrase attributed to him about the numbers three, six and nine.
licoes.a: Inside reading: Tesla was a real genius, with patents, engines and alternating current. Turning him into an esoteric prophet with made-up phrases is disrespectful of who he was. Practice: admire people for what they've really done.
licoes.c: To contemplate: do we need a genius to give permission to our intuition?

licoes.t: We only use 10% of the brain
p: we only use 10 percent of our brain
we only use 10% of the brain
licoes.r: Myth. Imaging shows that virtually all brain regions are functioning, and even during sleep many are active. Injuries in almost any area cause some damage. The brain uses about twenty percent of the body's energy; it would be impossible to keep a ninety percent useless organ.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the myth survives because it promises a hidden power to be unlocked. The truth is more useful: the potential is not in a dormant part, it's in how you use your whole brain, with attention, sleep and practice. Practice: Choose a skill and train 20 minutes a day for a week.
licoes.c: To contemplate: what power do you hope to gain from outside, that actually depends on training?

licoes.t: In the Middle Ages, they thought the Earth was flat.
p: in the middle ages, they thought the earth was flat
flat land in the middle ages
columbus proved that the earth is round
church said the earth was flat
na idade media achavam que a terra era plana
colombo provou que a terra e redonda
igreja dizia que a terra era plana
licoes.r: Myth. Since ancient Greece, scholars have known that the earth is spherical; Eratosthenes even calculated its circumference, about 240 B.C.E. In the Middle Ages, authors such as Bede and Thomas Aquinas wrote about the round Earth. The idea that everyone believed in a flat Earth until Columbus was popularized in the 19th century.
licoes.a: Inner reading: the myth serves to make us feel superior to the ancients. True humility is recognizing that people in the past also thought well, and that we also have our mistakes that the future will correct. Practice: learn an ancient discovery you didn't know.
licoes.c: To contemplate: which belief of today will look, five hundred years from now, like our flat Earth?

p: jesus was born on christmas day
licoes.r: The Gospels do not give the date of Jesus' birth; it is unknown. The earliest record of the celebration on December 25 in Rome is in the Chronograph of 354. Whether this date was chosen because of the feast of the Unconquered Sun or by a theological calculation is debated by historians; both explanations have defenders.
licoes.a: Inside reading: both sides exaggerate. Neither is the date a historical fact, nor is Christmas simply a pagan holiday in disguise. What's being celebrated is an idea: the light that rises on the longest night in the northern hemisphere. Practice: This Christmas, celebrate the birth of something new in you.
licoes.c: To ponder: Does the value of a symbol depend on the date being accurate?

p: constantine invented the divinity of jesus
nicene invented the divinity of jesus
constantino inventou a divindade de jesus
niceia inventou a divindade de jesus
licoes.r: Myth. Christianity existed almost three hundred years before Constantine, and many Christians already called Jesus God long before Nicaea: Ignatius of Antioch, about the year 110, does so in his letters. Constantine legalized Christianity in 313 and convened Nicaea in 325, where most bishops rejected Arius' thesis. He gave imperial power to the Church, and that changed a lot; but he didn't invent it.
licoes.a: Inside reading: What Constantine actually did is more important than the myth: the faith of the persecuted became the religion of the empire. That's where the blending of spirituality and power begins. Practice: always separate the message of a master from the use that power has made of it.
licoes.c: To ponder: what happens to a message of love when it wins an army?

licoes.t: Fluoride calcifies the pineal gland to block awakening.
p: fluoride calcifies the pineal gland to block awakening
licoes.r: Myth in the form in which it usually circulates. Calcification of the pineal gland is common and increases with age, and a small study from 2001 found accumulated fluoride in it. But there is no evidence that this blocks any spiritual capacity, nor of a plan for it. Fluoride in water, in the doses used, reduces cavities, according to the WHO.
licoes.a: Inner reading: The third eye, in traditions, is a symbol of inner vision, which develops with attention and silence, not with a fluoride-free diet. Seeking awakening in an external enemy is another form of the Matrix. Practice: Ten minutes of silence with your eyes closed is worth more than any detox.
licoes.c: To ponder: Is it easier to blame a conspiracy than to sit silently every day?

licoes.t: The Christians burned the Library of Alexandria
p: who burned the library of alexandria
fire of the library of alexandria
the christians burned the library of alexandria
quem queimou a biblioteca de alexandria
licoes.r: A simplification that became a myth. The Library of Alexandria did not disappear in a single fire: it declined over the centuries, with budget cuts, the expulsion of scholars in 145 B.C., and a fire in Julius Caesar's war in 48 B.C. In 391 C.E., Christians destroyed the Serapeum, a temple that housed part of a collection; it is not known how many books remained there.
licoes.a: Inside reading: the real story accuses several culprits and above all negligence, which kills knowledge slowly. A single villain is easier to hate, but less teachable. Practice: support a library, a teacher or an open knowledge project.
licoes.c: To contemplate: What knowledge is dying today, not by fire, but by neglect?

licoes.r: The vast majority of historians, believers and nonbelievers, accept that Jesus of Nazareth existed: a Jewish preacher from Galilee, baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate. In addition to the Gospels and Paul, he is mentioned by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus and by the Roman Tacitus. The thesis that he never existed is in the minority. Miracles and the resurrection are already a matter of faith, not history.
licoes.a: Inner reading: calculated truth separates what history holds, existence and crucifixion, from what is belief, miracles. That respects the believer and the skeptic at the same time. Practice: Read the Sermon on the Mount as the words of a real man, and see what they do for you.
licoes.c: To reflect: What changes in you if Jesus was a real man who said what he said?

licoes.r: Marguerite Porete was born around 1250, probably in the county of Hainaut, between France and the Holy Roman Empire. She was a highly educated woman and a beguine, one of the women who lived their faith freely, without convent vows and without a husband. She wrote The Mirror of Simple Souls and was burned alive in Paris on 1 June 1310.
licoes.a: Almost everything we know about her comes from the trial records, written by those who wanted to silence her. Even so, the portrait that remains is clear: a writer who dared to think about the sacred with her own mind and in the language of the people. No authentic portrait of her exists; the images in the memorial are artistic representations. Say Marguerite memorial to open the full page, with audio in Portuguese and English.
licoes.c: To contemplate: they kept her accusations, not her face. What part of you does the world only know through what others say about you?

licoes.r: In the 1290s Marguerite wrote, in Old French, the language of the people, and not in Latin, The Mirror of Simple and Annihilated Souls. It is a dialogue between the Soul, Love and Reason. The Soul passes through seven states until it lets go of everything that is only its own and becomes transparent, like a mirror, to divine love.
licoes.a: She calls this annihilation: not the death of the person, but the end of the prison of the ego. Such a soul no longer lives out of fear of punishment or by trading favours with heaven; it lives free, because it loves. In chapter 22 she compares the free soul to the eagle, which flies higher than all other birds. For the power of that time, this freedom was the danger: whoever finds God through love no longer depends on intermediaries.
licoes.c: To contemplate: what would you need to let go of to become transparent like a mirror? Fear, pride, the need to be right?

licoes.r: Between 1296 and 1306 the bishop of Cambrai had the book burned in public in Valenciennes, in front of her. She did not obey the ban. Around 1308 she was arrested and handed over to the inquisitor of France, the Dominican William of Paris, the same man behind the trial of the Templars. She spent about a year and a half in prison and refused to take the oath or to answer.
licoes.a: Unable to question her, the inquisitors put the book on trial. They took fifteen sentences from it, the articles, and in April 1310 twenty-one theologians of the University of Paris declared them heretical. Today only three of the fifteen articles can be identified with certainty. Because she had kept spreading a book already condemned, she was declared a relapsed heretic. Earlier, three churchmen, among them Godfrey of Fontaines, a master of theology in Paris, had approved the text.
licoes.c: To contemplate: her silence was her defence. When is silence stronger than explaining yourself?

p: a mulher que sorriu na fogueira
licoes.r: On 1 June 1310, at the Place de Grève in Paris, where the City Hall square is today, Marguerite Porete was burned alive. She did not recant. The continuation of the chronicle of Guillaume de Nangis, written by someone with no sympathy for her, recorded that she faced death so calmly that the crowd wept.
licoes.a: About the phrase the woman who smiled at the stake: the sources speak of calm and serenity, and say the people wept; no source of the time says she smiled. The smile is a poetic reading of that peace. The beguin Guiard de Cressonessart, who tried to defend her, confessed under pressure and was sentenced to life in prison. They burned the woman; they could not burn what she had understood.
licoes.c: To contemplate: what kind of peace lets someone face the fire without hatred? Where does a calm come from that does not depend on what happens outside?
s: After the fire: the nameless book
Victims of the Inquisition: the memorial

licoes.t: After the fire: the nameless book
p: after the fire the nameless book
licoes.r: The book survived without her name. It was copied and translated into Latin, Italian and Middle English, and travelled through several countries, read by monks and nuns who did not know they were reading a condemned woman. Only in 1946 did the Italian historian Romana Guarnieri recognise Marguerite Porete's book in Latin manuscripts of the Vatican Library.
licoes.a: Before that, the Mirror was even attributed to other authors, and in 1927 it was printed in English as the work of an unknown French mystic, in Clare Kirchberger's edition. Six hundred and thirty-six years after the fire, she got her own name back.
licoes.c: To contemplate: her ideas travelled for centuries without a signature. Does a truth need the name of whoever said it to stay alive?

licoes.t: Victims of the Inquisition: the memorial
p: victims of the inquisition the memorial
how many did the inquisition kill
licoes.r: Marguerite was not the only one. Historians estimate that the Spanish Inquisition prosecuted about one hundred and fifty thousand people and sent between three thousand and five thousand to their deaths. The Portuguese Inquisition, which also reached Brazil, burned at least one thousand one hundred and seventy-five people alive, according to Henry Charles Lea.
licoes.a: Among the victims of the Portuguese Inquisition was the Rio-born playwright Antônio José da Silva, executed in Lisbon in 1739. In Europe's witch hunts, driven by church courts and also by secular courts, Catholic and Protestant alike, between forty thousand and sixty thousand people were executed, most of them women. Historians themselves warn that these numbers are minimums: many deaths in prison and under torture were never recorded.
licoes.c: To contemplate: behind every number there is a name and a silenced voice. You do not need to despise believers to see this; many sincere believers were victims too. What can you do today so that no conscience is locked away?

licoes.r: The memorial has a text written as a tribute, as if she were speaking. Note: it is an imagined text, not a historical speech. It begins: I am Marguerite. I have no portrait; nobody painted my face. They kept only the accusations against me. But I left a mirror.
licoes.a: And it ends: My name is Marguerite, and through my name speak thousands who could not finish their sentence. Finish it for us. Think freely. Love without fear. Her real words are in the book. In chapter 6 the Soul says: Virtues, I take leave of you for evermore; now shall mine heart be more free and more in peace. And in chapter 22 the free soul is compared to the eagle, which flies higher than any other bird.
licoes.c: To contemplate: if you could leave a single sentence to those who come after you, what would it be?

licoes.r: The original book can be downloaded for free, in public-domain editions only: the fifteenth-century Chantilly manuscript, as a two-hundred-and-fifty-six-page PDF on Wikimedia Commons; the full Middle French text transcribed by Wikisource; and the medieval English translation published in 1927, on the Internet Archive.
licoes.a: The links are in the memorial, in the section The book, and in the sources of this lesson. The Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA 4.0 and is stored in the app to read offline. Modern translations are under copyright, so they are listed only as references, without files.
licoes.c: To contemplate: reading the original source, even slowly, is an act of freedom. Which book do you only know from what others said about it?
s: After the fire: the nameless book

licoes.r: Marguerite's story asks each of us: who has the right to decide what you may think, read, write and feel about the sacred? For centuries, institutions that claimed to speak in God's name used fear, fire and silence to control consciences.
licoes.a: What is denounced here is not sincere faith, but dogma armed with power, the idea that truth needs jailers. Freedom of conscience, of thought and of knowledge was won with lives like hers. Every time someone thinks for themselves, asks without fear and shares what they learned, Marguerite's flame stays lit, not as a fire, but as light.
licoes.c: To contemplate: on what subject do you still ask permission to think?
s: Victims of the Inquisition: the memorial
